title: 'Penelope' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Self-financing is an anomaly in TV, which doesn’t have the same infrastructure to support independent production as film. But in the case of 2024’s Penelope, it was the only option that allowed creators Mark Duplass and Mel Eslyn the freedom to make the unprecedented work they envisioned. As Duplass explained in interviews, when they pitched the half-hour drama about a girl who runs away from an apparently normal 16-year-old life to tough out a Thoreauvian existence in Cascade National Forest, the response from many execs was: “This is beautiful and unique and poetic, and are you crazy, we can’t make it unless there’s a murder in the first 30 seconds!” Which pretty much sums up the current streaming marketplace. Happily, the indie-cinema veterans had the means to produce the series—a lyrical, often wordless portrait of the spiritual seeker as a young woman, soulfully portrayed by Megan Stott. Because it never fully explains itself, Penelope suggests many resonant interpretations. It shows us a teen girl driven by a thirst for freedom rather than love or social status. It has environmental overtones. It feels representative of a tech-saturated generation’s longing to liberate itself from algorithms, surveillance, the attention economy. Yet the show, eventually licensed by Netflix, seems meant to be experienced more than analyzed. Like silent meditation or a hike in the wilderness, it’s a chance to run some fresh air through your 21st-century brain and see what detritus it displaces.

title: 'Slip' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Science fiction doesn’t have to be all spaceships and robots. A romantic comedy also can be weird as hell. And the Roku Channel, it turns out, can be a platform for great original programs. Slip contains all of these unlikely truths (although, as of the summer of 2026, the three-year-old show has moved from Roku to Peacock). Creator Zoe Lister-Jones stars as Mae, an urbanite at a marital impasse, looking ahead to a future that promises only domestic stagnation. Instead of sending her into a customary shame spiral, a desperate act of infidelity launches Mae into a full-on alternate universe where she’s married to the previous night’s hookup. When she tries to fix it by sleeping with someone else, she wakes up with that person as a life partner. And so on through wildly divergent spousal scenarios, featuring such welcome faces as The Decameron dreamboat Amar Chadha-Patel and Emily Hampshire from Schitt’s Creek. Though Mae’s succession of parallel lives is well-suited to television’s episodic structure, Slip is the rare show that feels like a small-screen equivalent to the cool, character-driven indie movies that make up most of Lister-Jones’ filmography. High-concept but low-key, it’s an insightful meditation on adult relationships that doesn’t take itself too seriously.

title: 'Men of a Certain Age' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Won’t somebody think of the middle-aged men? I kid, I kid. In truth, the friendships and inner lives of men young, old, and in between are chronically ignored by Hollywood, which would rather see even the elderly among them blow up bad guys than admit to having feelings. And so I would like to think that this sensitive dramedy about three best buddies pushing 50 reached a smaller audience than it deserved not because of its gentle subject matter, but because it was hidden away in the procedural wasteland of late-aughts TNT. Created by Ray Romano and Mike Royce, Men of a Certain Age finds each of its flawed but likable leads in the midst of a midlife crisis. Romano’s wry, hangdog default demeanor suits his character, Joe, a father of two who’s separated from his wife (Penelope Ann Miller) and living in a depressing motel. Once an aspiring pro golfer, he has settled for owning a party-supply store and nursing a sports-gambling habit. Lifelong bachelor Terry (Scott Bakula) can feel himself aging out of his womanizing years as well as his acting career. The real standout among the exceptional cast, though, is the late Andre Braugher as Owen, a diabetic who works a job he hates, selling cars at his hypercompetitive dad’s (Richard Gant) dealership, to support the wife (LisaGay Hamilton) and kids he loves. His tenderness and vulnerability sets the tone of the show, which takes men’s emotions seriously without lapsing into either the preachy hugging and learning of Ted Lasso or the manipulative melodramatics of, say, A Million Little Pieces. Some of the best scenes are just Owen, Joe, and Terry sharing a meal at their favorite diner, talking openly—and good-naturedly busting each other’s chops—about whatever happens to be going on in their lives.

title: 'It's a Sin' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: No TV program since Angels in America captured the scope and pain of the early AIDS crisis like this five-part drama from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies. But when it comes to style, tone, and personnel, the miniseries are about as different as two stories about the same plague can be. While Mike Nichols’ 2003 HBO adaptation of Tony Kushner’s Pulitzer-winning play was epic in every sense, from its spiritual grandeur to a cast led by Al Pacino and Meryl Streep, It’s a Sin—which made a splash on Channel 4 in the U.K. but barely seemed to ripple on HBO Max in the U.S.—thrived on intimacy. Spanning the decade between 1981 and 1991, it follows a group of initially college-aged queer men and their friends as they leave mostly intolerant homes and converge on London. The experience is exhilarating at first: clubs, parties, hookups, liberation, community. Then come the reports of a “gay cancer” afflicting otherwise healthy young men in New York and San Francisco. Inevitably, the epidemic crosses the ocean, taking the lives of some characters and turning others into dogged activists. It’s the vividness and verisimilitude with which these fictional people are drawn that make the show unforgettable. (Olly Alexander and Lydia West are especially great as, respectively, a theatrical loudmouth and his earnest best friend.) Before we get to know them as tragic figures, they are witty and artistic and innocent and curious. Those qualities don’t disappear once disaster strikes. They must, however, coexist with the rightful anger that creeps into later episodes, as individual and systemic homophobia exacerbates an already catastrophic situation. This turn made It’s a Sin a welcome corrective to the many AIDS narratives that have been quick to forgive the bigotry of the past—and to forget that silence really did equal death.

title: 'Downward Dog' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: With a few wonderful exceptions that proved the rule (The Good Place, New Girl), the network sitcom landscape of the 2010s was a graveyard of glib titles, gimmicky premises, and mercifully short runs. (Remember CBS’s, er, Twitter account adaptation Sh*! My Dad Says? Or ABC’s noxious attempt at mancession-sploitation Work It?) At first glance, Downward Dog looked like more of the same. Its narrator is a dog named Martin, voiced by co-creator Samm Hodges, who expounds on his philosophies of life and analyzes from a uniquely canine perspective his relationship with his owner, Nan (Allison Tolman), whose corporate career is increasingly cutting into their time together. Yet there is, surprisingly, nothing cynical about the show. Its charm is, in large part, a credit to Tolman. Fresh off an Emmy-nominated performance as the archetypal good cop in the first season of Fargo, she brought that same sense of beleaguered decency to this stressed-out character. Downward Dog also distinguished itself from dozens of broad, jokey, try-hard broadcast comedies with its more laid-back, gentle but never cloying tone. Alas, with so many other programs clamoring for eyeballs, these subtle pleasures failed to draw an audience big enough to keep it on the air after its initial eight-episode season. But the show remains an ideal comfort watch. And, happily, we can now enjoy Tolman in a successful sitcom worthy of her kind presence: NBC’s hospital mockumentary St. Denis Medical.

title: 'Crashing' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Phoebe Waller-Bridge is the most celebrated British TV creator of her generation. Her blistering 2016 traumedy Fleabag broke big the moment it crossed the Atlantic via co-producer Prime Video, fueling rapturous reviews and spirited discourse about the comedy of female sexuality. A few years later, the surprisingly metaphysical second season dominated the Emmys, made “Hot Priest” Andrew Scott a sex symbol, and even got a shout-out from Barack Obama. In between the two installments, Waller-Bridge found time to helm the beloved first season of the smart-pulp espionage thriller Killing Eve. And yet, few people seem to have encountered Crashing, her deeply enjoyable comedy that debuted the same year as Fleabag. Lighter than the latter show and less violent than Eve, it centers around six young adults living as property guardians (that is, temporary residents who pay minimal rent in exchange for keeping out squatters) in a disused hospital. The crumbling institution makes an appropriately strange backdrop for a romp that mixes madcap antics, tangled romantic relationships, and the frank, sometimes enthusiastically gross sexuality that is one of Waller-Bridge’s signatures. The cast features not just the creator, who makes the Manic Pixie Dream Girl archetype her own as ukulele troubadour Lulu, but also a pre-Bridgerton Jonathan Bailey in the wild role of an inveterate womanizer. This might all remind you of a certain famous hangout sitcom millennials grew up watching. But trust me when I promise you that Waller-Bridge was well aware of what came before and didn’t take any of Crashing’s storylines in a remotely predictable direction.

title: 'Bupkis' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Pete Davidson is either the luckiest man in Hollywood or a guy cursed with an undeserved bad rap. Few seem to have moderate opinions on the comedian, and how you view him likely depends on how much of his fame you attribute to innate talent and how much you write him off as a cynically self-dramatizing zillennial, milking his drug issues, mental health struggles, and parade of superstar girlfriends for attention. His short-lived 2023 Peacock comedy Bupkis offered evidence for both sides, beginning with a sophomoric groaner of a premiere that you should absolutely skip. If you move on to the rest, though, you’ll find a disarmingly thoughtful, semi-autobiographical show that interrogates the bizarre experience of 21st century infamy through the hooded eyes of a man uniquely qualified to speak on the subject. One episode puts Pete in conversation with John Mulaney, who also appears as himself, about their very different reputations. Another finds his misery exacerbated by a Christmas spent shooting a war movie opposite its star Brad Pitt’s stand-in, in a rare evocation of how impersonal blockbuster filmmaking has become. While it works better on an episodic basis than as a season-length statement, Bupkis deserves a bigger audience than it initially found. For all that has been said about him in the media, Davidson has a clearer perspective than anyone on what his actual problems are. His insights into topics like substance abuse, persona, and family go beyond navel-gazing. And speaking of family: Italian American screen icons Edie Falco and Joe Pesci play his mom and grandfather. Come for that cast, stay to develop a true appreciation for a man who helped inspire “thank u, next.”

title: 'This Fool' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: A whole subgenre of sitcoms revolves around odd couples: Felix and Oscar, Abbi and Ilana, Liz Lemon and Jack Donaghy. Just as deserving of a place in that canon are Julio (co-creator Chris Estrada) and Luis (Frankie Quiñones), the cousins at the center of the uproarious two-season Hulu comedy This Fool (2022-2023). When they were kids, mischievous Luis bullied geeky Julio. Now, Luis is a former gang member who’s just been released from prison and Julio works for a nonprofit, Hugs Not Thugs, that helps people like Luis. Which is not to say that Julio is thriving, either; the perpetually morose protagonist still lives with his mom (Laura Patalano) and grandmother (Julia Vera) in the family’s South Central L.A. home and is stuck in a holding pattern with his longtime girlfriend (Michelle Ortiz). Along with skewering the criminal justice system through Hugs Not Thugs—whose radical leftist founder is played to strident perfection by Michael Imperioli—Estrada immerses viewers in the textures of and tensions within the cousins’ multicultural neighborhood. Yet what makes the show stand out is how many laughs it packs into each episode, especially in an era of dark dramedies and mainstream sitcoms that just aren’t that funny. From wild plots and lived-in character comedy to sly satire, slapstick, and unrepentant raunch, This Fool excels on every level.

title: 'We Are Lady Parts' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: For every identity that is stereotyped or marginalized in mainstream pop culture, there are thousands, if not millions, of very different people whose individuality gets erased in the process. Muslim women, for example. So what better way to counter decades of representational flattening than with a show whose central characters are young Londoners who share that label but little besides it—and then throw them together in a punk band? The result is We Are Lady Parts, a raucous British comedy that premiered in 2021 and whose two seasons were co-produced by Channel 4 and Peacock. (At the moment, it’s not clear whether we can expect a third.) Among creator Nida Manzoor’s richly written characters, all vividly portrayed by a cast with real chemistry, are a chill mom and artist (Faith Omole), a frontwoman (Sarah Kameela Impey) with riot-grrrl rage and a day job as a halal butcher, and an anxious engineering grad student in search of an arranged marriage (Anjana Vasan). From their personalities and styles to their ethnic backgrounds, sexual orientations, and relationships to Islam, these women couldn’t be more different. Yet Manzoor is never didactic about expanding viewers’ perceptions of Muslim women. She’s here to rock and to make us laugh, often at the same time, with subversive original songs (“Voldemort Under My Headscarf,” “Malala Made Me Do It”) catchy and clever enough to anchor any pop-punk playlist.

title: 'Such Brave Girls' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: If you can’t beat the trauma plot that has come to dominate narrative art forms, you might as well get exceedingly weird and exuberantly dark with it. That seems to be the theory, anyway, behind this British black comedy about a family of women desperate to appease—but already driven mad by—the patriarchal forces that control their lives. Creator Kat Sadler’s awkward 20-something protagonist, Josie, is a closeted lesbian whose clingy boyfriend (Freddie Meredith) cheerfully ignores the disgust she radiates. Her delusional younger sister, Billie (played by Sadler’s real-life sister, Lizzie Davidson), has a habit of throwing herself at the most inappropriate men available. Where did they learn these deranged behaviors? From their mother, of course! Abandoned by the girls’ dad, Deb (Louise Brealey) channels all her obsessive energy into locking down a man with the means to rescue them from destitution. Loony antics ensue. While Such Brave Girls was anointed with a BAFTA for the first of its two seasons to date, which premiered in 2023, it’s barely been noticed Stateside, despite being readily available on Hulu. The show’s send-up of heteropessimist humiliation might feel a bit harsh to a population for whom the British Office couldn’t be adapted without a thorough defanging. Still, Americans who like their cringe comedy laceratingly scripted and spiked with existential despair should give it a try.

title: 'Rain Dogs' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Shows about chosen family tend to be a bit saccharine—bless these beautiful misfits going out into the world and finding in each other the love and support their awful parents never gave them! Not Rain Dogs. This tart 2023 British dramedy takes a scalpel to the codependent relationship between Costello (Daisy May Cooper), a destitute peep-show dancer and single mum who dreams of becoming a writer, and her manipulative best friend, Selby (Jack Farthing), an upper-class gay man who just got out of prison. First-time creator Cash Carraway depicts the two leads’ destructive tendencies without cliché. Particularly harrowing is the threat Costello’s thrall to Selby seems to pose to her daughter, Iris (Fleur Tashjian). Yet he loves the little girl, too, to the extent that love is possible for a sadist of his magnitude. Along with darkly witty dialogue that shares a sensibility with gutter poets like Jean Genet and Tom Waits (whose song and album give the show its title), as well as Cooper and Farthing’s almost spookily complete embodiment of their broken characters, it is the genuineness of these three people’s longing to be a family that keeps Rain Dogs from sinking into despair. Underpublicized during its Stateside run on HBO, this is TV with the emotional immediacy of live theater, so do as you would at a Broadway show, silence your phone before pressing play.

title: 'My Mad Fat Diary' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Oh, to have been 16 years old in mid-1990s England, when Britpop had gone global, the U.K. was the center of the pop-culture universe, and the word Brexit meant nothing to anyone. It sounds like a blast, but not all Cool Britannia comings-of-age were created equal. Based on Rae Earl’s 2007 memoir in diary entries, this 2013 drama follows a depressive, 231-lb., working-class high school girl who, when we meet her, has just been released from a psychiatric institution following a suicide attempt. Yet it’s anything but a downbeat drag. Rae, portrayed with remarkable sensitivity by Sharon Rooney, is at heart a sensualist yearning for community and pleasure, and the show’s emotional intensity reflects that often-frustrated lust for life. Her first taste of reciprocation comes via her gorgeous best friend, Chloe (Jodie Comer in an early role), who initiates her into a fun-loving coed clique. Unlike the typical TV fat girl, she gets the kind of swooning romance arc that YouTube montages are made of. As Rae and her crew bond, wallow, and heal through the songs that mean everything to them, that music—Oasis, Blur, Radiohead, Portishead—soundtracks their every rite of passage. If you were there (or wished you were), prepare to feel the rush of nostalgia. And if not? A new world of “Champagne Supernova” sing-alongs and extremely specific teen angst awaits.

title: 'Lenox Hill' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: If you ever had any doubt that working in a hospital can be as intense as it looks on The Pitt, Lenox Hill will quickly dispel it. A rare serious documentary about health care workers in a medium that never stops putting new twists on the doctor-drama format, this series from director-producers Ruthie Shatz and Adi Barash follows four physicians at Manhattan’s Lenox Hill Hospital. Two are high-ranking male neurosurgeons who must balance high-wire cases, research interests, tough conversations with patients and their families, and the suite of administrative tasks that come with their leadership roles. In a fascinating contrast, the other two subjects are busy, thoughtful female doctors of color, one an OBGYN and one an ER practitioner, who both happened to be pregnant while the series was taping. Shatz and Barash resist imposing a tight structure; episodes flow between subjects and departments, allowing viewers to get a sense of their respective rhythms. And then, in a finale that revisits the Lenox Hill team at the height of New York’s nightmarish 2020 COVID outbreak, we watch people who were already giving 100% on the job find the fortitude to push even harder through the crisis. But the urgency of Lenox Hill didn’t end with the pandemic. One of the most universal issues of our time, health care is also among the most opaque. Each vignette in this emotional series casts new light on its personnel, procedures, and pain points, clarifying the life-or-death stakes of quality care and reminding us that Dr. Robby has real-life counterparts in every city.

title: 'First Person' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: No documentarian has a better eye for intriguing oddballs than Errol Morris, who built his feature film career on drawing them out in conversation, from pet-cemetery owners in Gates of Heaven to small-town eccentrics in Vernon, Florida. Morris brought his profiling skills to a pre-Housewives Bravo with First Person, released at the turn of the millennium and difficult to find in the streaming era before the filmmaker uploaded it to his YouTube page during the pandemic. Each half-hour episode consists of a single, wide-ranging interview with someone whose name viewers probably didn’t recognize, but whose story was gripping—a Unabomber confidant, a CIA alum who specialized in disguises, a bouncer who claims to have a higher IQ than Einstein. The show’s best-known subject is probably its first, Temple Grandin, whose devotion to making livestock slaughter humane leads to an insightful discussion of mortality. But, as always, Morris finds profundity in unexpected places. “When I was growing up, I was very comfortable in my absolutes,” mob lawyer Murray Richman reflects, by way of explaining how he became an extreme moral relativist. “I believed in God, I believed in my country, I believed in my parents.” Now? “My parents are dead, God doesn’t exist, and the country’s full of crap. What’s left?” In 2026, First Person would likely have been a TikTok account or a podcast. There’s value, though, in the visual elements of Morris’s interviews as well as their extended length. Both help make the case that unfamous people, in all their honesty and complexity, are as worthy of our attention as celebrities.

title: 'Dead Like Me' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Bryan Fuller is the king of the brilliant but canceled show. In the middle of a career bookended by Star Trek series, he made two bona fide cult classics: the stylish, homoerotic Silence of the Lambs prequel Hannibal and Pushing Daisies, a procedural about a man who uses his power of reanimation to solve murder cases. But his angsty-young-woman period, which yielded 2003’s Dead Like Me as well as 2004’s currently-unavailable-in-any-digital-format Wonderfalls, could use more retrospective love. A supernatural Showtime dramedy that bears many Fuller signatures—a far-out premise, quirky characters, sarcastic dialogue—Dead cast Ellen Muth in what should have been a star-making role as George Lass, a disaffected college dropout who dies in the very first episode. Instead of getting beamed up to the afterlife, George remains on Earth, having been chosen, for unknown reasons, as one of many undead “reapers” who collect human souls just before they die. She’s absorbed into a ragtag reaper crew, led by an avuncular Mandy Patinkin (whose presence should be enough to get anyone to watch any show), that hangs out at a German-themed diner. As she adjusts to a depressing vocation she really doesn’t want, George has to hold down an office job (the Almighty doesn’t pay a salary), emotionally disentangle herself from her mourning family, and finish the growing-up process she barely started in life. It’s a lot of moving parts for one show; the double-workplace-comedy and undead-coming-of-age elements work better than the somewhat generic family drama. Still, it’s far more enjoyable—comforting, even—than any series about dying young has any right to be.

title: 'China, IL' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Cable’s home for adult animation (and offbeat live-action comedies), Cartoon Network’s Adult Swim programming block is a cult-TV factory. Tim and Eric, The Boondocks, Aqua Teen Hunger Force, The Eric Andre Show—they all have outspoken fan bases. Rick and Morty has such an enormous and obsessive following, it might be the biggest cult show of all time. But not every Adult Swim gem gets the decade-plus run that its signature hits often enjoy, and some standout titles ultimately drop off the radar of even the brand’s core audience. Such has been the case for China, IL, a cartoon that had a long, web-based prehistory before leveling up to series status in 2011. Created by Brad Neely, a comics artist and creative polymath known for his beloved alternate Harry Potter soundtrack, the pastel-hued oddity uses a state university populated by petty, neurotic academics as a backdrop for all sorts of fantastical hilarity. The time-traveling premiere, which humiliates both Reagan and Hitler, is sure to weed out anyone unsuited to Neely’s rude, lewd, manically referential style of humor. But if it makes you chuckle, you’ll probably also delight in the episode where the science lab produces a baby the size of a building and the one that has a secret society of bored professors downing a potion that transforms them into orgy-prone forest creatures. This brand of comedy is perfectly suited to Adult Swim’s signature joke-dense, 11-minute format. And in case you weren’t aware, China, IL is just one of dozens of shows, new and old, streaming for free on the brand’s website.

title: 'Betty' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated Shows
full_text: In the canon of teen entertainment, boys tend to make mischief while girls give each other makeovers. One great pleasure of Betty—creator Crystal Moselle’s expansion of her 2018 indie feature Skate Kitchen—is how it defies that binary simply by ignoring it. Fictionalizing the adventures of a real, all-female New York City skateboard crew, whose members also dominated its cast, the show luxuriates in images of girls bonding (and sometimes beefing) through roguish behavior: daredevil skating, drug experimentation, picking fights, chasing love interests of one gender or another. Betty defies genre; while episodes run half an hour and the banter can be hilarious, many of the situations and themes it touches, from race and class privilege to sexual assault, are quite serious. Moselle’s dreamy style allows these seemingly disparate elements to melt together in generous, wordless skate-park footage, as fluid and kinetic as a sunny afternoon spent wandering the Lower East Side with a pack of friends and no particular agenda. For New Yorkers who love it, the show holds special meaning because it debuted in the long lockdown spring of 2020 and gave back to us a vision of a vibrant city we missed terribly. Yet you don’t have to know the street corners where artsy lovergirl Honeybear (Kabrina “Moonbear” Adams) and goofy, pugnacious Kirt (Nina Moran) lean against hydrants to appreciate the magic of Betty. At its core, it’s a celebration of youthful freedom, and that’s universal.

title: 'Work in Progress' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Showtime’s Work in Progress sounds, on paper, like the show a right-wing cultural warrior would make up to caricature the “woke” entertainment industry. Comedian Abby McEnany stars in this semi-autobiographical series as a suicidal, middle-aged, self-described “fat... queer dyke who hasn’t done sh-t in her life.” Her healing journey involves dating a 20-something trans man (Theo Germaine) and confronting SNL alum Julia Sweeney, whose androgynous character Pat bears a humiliating resemblance to Abby. The thing is, McEnany, co-creator Tim Mason, and a team of executive producers that included Lilly Wachowski as well as Sweeney immediately subvert any expectation of a sanctimonious or self-serious exploration of identity. As executed, the 2019 show is an emotional yet refreshingly unsentimental black comedy that snickers in the face of empowerment buzzwords like, well, healing journey. In its frustratingly brief, two-season run, Work in Progress expanded outward from Abby’s immediate crisis, using everything from childhood flashbacks to the societal reset of COVID-19 to interrogate—often hilariously—how a person might come to feel so lonely and desperate at a stage of life when we’re expected to have everything figured out. Fans of HBO’s Somebody Somewhere will definitely see parallels here. But really, Abby’s plight should be relatable to anyone who doesn’t pre-judge her for leading with her identity. The midlife crisis is, after all, a tale as old as Dante.

title: 'Underground' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: In the mid-2010s, with streaming services on the rise and the future of cable uncertain, networks that had long relied on licensed programming scrambled to develop high-quality original series that might justify their continued existence. Although the prestige strategy couldn’t save WGN America, which is now NewsNation, it did yield a few good dramas. The best of these was 2016’s Underground, a historical thriller set in the years leading up to the Civil War. At its center is a group of enslaved people planning an escape from a Georgia plantation. But creators Misha Green (who would go on to make HBO’s Lovecraft Country) and Joe Pokaski (Cloak & Dagger) broadened its scope to examine many aspects of slavery and the Underground Railroad. A superb cast featuring Jurnee Smollett, Aldis Hodge, and Christopher Meloni portrays white abolitionists, free Black people, and devious bounty hunters. Unlike Barry Jenkins’ auteurist adaptation of Colson Whitehead’s The Underground Railroad, this is generally a fast-paced, plot-driven show, propelled by action and romance. (There is also a lot of graphic, racist violence that some viewers might find hard to stomach.) Yet it can also be remarkably perceptive about the far-reaching moral implications of slavery, which made all of white America complicit and fueled bigotry even among those who opposed it. Green and Pokaski took some bold creative risks, too. One of Underground’s most memorable episodes consists entirely of an electrifying speech by Harriet Tubman (Aisha Hinds) to a crowd of northern abolitionists.

title: 'The Bisexual' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: As terrifying as an unwritten future can be, there’s something equally scary about certainty. You just rarely see the latter explored in the millennial dramedies that proliferated a decade or so ago. The Bisexual, a Channel 4-Hulu co-production created by the filmmaker Desiree Akhavan (Appropriate Behavior, The Miseducation of Cameron Post) and Rowan Riley, took on that underexplored idea. Akhavan stars as Leila, a young woman who has spent essentially her entire adult life in a relationship with a much-older girlfriend, Sadie (Maxine Peake), who wants to marry Leila. To make the situation even more claustrophobic, they run a start-up together. Sensing she has one last chance to form an identity separate from Sadie, restless Leila seizes it, moving out for a trial separation and renting a room from the kind of straight, white, male novelist (Brian Gleeson) who shrugs off Zadie Smith as “not untalented” and sleeps with his students. As she squabbles with the circle of queer, female friends who are aghast at her for leaving Sadie, Leila—who has always identified as a lesbian and never had sex with a guy—begins exploring her curiosity about men. Female sexual fluidity can be a delicate subject. Sleeping with a woman like Leila is the male fantasy that launched a thousand porn movies, and many lesbians, particularly those of Sadie’s generation, dismiss bisexual women as dabbling straights. Yet Akhavan’s self-aware script acknowledges all of this baggage without letting it weigh down what is, in large part, a comedy of late-stage growing up, with a main character too specific to use as the basis for generalizations. The whole supporting cast is great, but look out for Saskia Chana as Leila’s best friend Deniz, a fount of withering lines delivered with deadpan panache.

title: 'On Becoming a God in Central Florida' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: The holders of TV’s purse strings are constantly breaking my heart, and probably yours as well, with premature cancellations. But when Showtime renewed On Becoming a God in Central Florida for a second season only to axe it after COVID delayed production of the new episodes? That really stung. While the Kirsten Dunst dramedy’s central ideas—Florida as microcosm for America, pyramid schemes as metaphor for the American Dream—weren’t exactly groundbreaking, first-time creators Robert Funke and Matt Lusky and showrunner Esta Spalding used those themes less as a didactic destination and more as a backdrop for magnificent, character-rich mayhem. Dunst’s Krystal Stubbs is a fireball of a mom and water-park employee in early-’90s suburban Orlando, who gets dragged into a multilevel-marketing mess that her worthless, delusional husband, Travis (Alexander Skarsgård), has convinced himself will make them rich. Of course, it takes a truly extraordinary person to wring success out of such a scam, and while that’s certainly not Travis, Krystal’s combination of ambition, energy, and desperation soon propel her to rising-star status in the scheme’s cultish community. Surrounding her as she grinds is a colorful but authentic assortment of strivers played by character actor par excellence Mel Rodriguez, Gossip frontwoman Beth Ditto, and future Lurker star Théodore Pellerin.Krystal and her associates’ yearning to replace their precarious lives with the affluent, secure ones that hard work was supposed to earn them feels as relatable as, for most Americans, it really is.

title: 'Sherman’s Showcase' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: In the years immediately before streaming crowded out niche cable channels, IFC was TV’s home for affectionate, weirdly specific pop-culture parodies. It had Portlandia sending up hipsters and Documentary Now! spoofing nonfiction cinema. Though it came unluckily late in that run, airing from 2019 through 2022, Sherman’s Showcase deserves a place in the cult-classic comedy canon alongside those predecessors. Created by Bashir Salahuddin and Diallo Riddle—the late-night alums behind Comedy Central’s also-underappreciated sitcom South Side—it casts Salahuddin as the extravagantly flawed host of a long-running variety show in the Soul Train vein. Its framing, as a series of promotional retrospectives looking back on aspects of Showcase’s legacy, allows each episode to leapfrog through time, dropping in on the music, style, gossip, and adversity that defined specific moments in Black culture. What really made the show special were its wild imagination, cultural-studies-PhD-level knowledge of its subject, and stunning roster of guest stars, to say nothing of the density of jokes. A fashion episode, hosted by Eliza Coupe doing an unhinged accent as “Mrs. Hungarian-Germanic-Swede 1998,” features Issa Rae as Iman, an Ocean’s 8 riff that has Mary J. Blige (Bresha Webb) masterminding an all-female heist of Diddy’s compound, a spot-on Wes Anderson spoof that doubles as an alternate history of Reconstruction, and a diabolical cameo from executive producer John Legend. Incredibly, just about every half-hour of Showcase’s two-season run is equally inspired.

title: 'Made for Love' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: What must it be like to marry a top-tier tech mogul, the kind of guy who not only has billions in the bank, but also possesses enough personal data or supply-chain control to exert godlike power over the average person? This question animated Alissa Nutting’s 2017 novel Made for Love and the 2021 sci-fi black comedy series of the same name she co-created for HBO Max. Cristin Milioti was in her sweet spot as lovable mess Hazel, who left college a decade ago to marry tech titan Byron Gogol (Billy Magnussen), a control-freak inventor whose toxic quirks evoke many real-world counterparts. She’s spent those years effectively accepting that she’s trapped in the holographically shape-shifting compound where her husband lives and works. But when she finally snaps and escapes, she learns that Byron has implanted a device in her brain that gives him access to her consciousness. With nowhere else to go, she winds up at the shabby home of her estranged dad, Herbert (Ray Romano, rounding out a fantastic lead trio). Of course, because Byron is a psycho with terrifying surveillance capabilities and unlimited resources, Hazel has an easier time getting free than staying free. Finding humor in tech anxiety, economic polarization, and the search for love in a lonely era (Herbert has replaced Hazel’s late mom with a sex doll), Made for Love handled its themes a bit too breezily at first. By its second and final season, however, the show had evolved into just as dark, audacious, and profound a satire as Nutting’s brilliant book. It’s only gotten more trenchant since its premature cancellation and removal from the HBO Max library, as AI invades our minds and the Byrons of the world consolidate their power.

title: 'Corporate' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Any consumer with rudimentary critical-thinking skills will occasionally encounter a breathtakingly cynical bit of promo propaganda, and wonder: What kind of monster came up with this? Corporate, an undersung artifact of the bygone era when Comedy Central made its own live-action, scripted comedies (specifically, the late 2010s), was a veritable bestiary of such ghouls. Set within the offices of fictional megacorp Hampton DeVille (slogan: “We make everything”), the show filtered its satire through the Kafkaesque perspectives of two drones (Matt Ingebretson and Jake Weisman, who created Corporate with director Pat Bishop) doomed to be permanent “junior executives in training.” Life has beaten down Weisman’s Jake Levinson, once the radical front man of a bad Rage Against the Machine clone, into a dead-eyed nihilist. Ingebretson’s Matt Engelbertson still holds out hope of a brilliant career, despite all feedback to the contrary from the joined-at-the-lapel demons of officiousness who are their supervisors (Anne Dudek and Adam Lustick). The late Lance Reddick is a delight in one of his final roles, as their diabolical CEO. And Aparna Nancherla warms up the ice-cold cast of characters as Matt and Jake’s sympathetic but powerless buddy in HR. Along with product and branding ideas straight out of the Shark Tank reject bin, the show’s humor is grounded in sharp observations about big corporations’ contempt for their customers and how desperate they are, at the same time, to make us believe they care.

title: 'Don’t Trust the B—- in Apartment 23' Is One of TIME's 50 Most Underappreciated TV Shows
full_text: Beginning in the mid-2000s, a horde of ambitious millennial women raised on Friends and Sex and the City descended on New York to seize the glamorous careers, palatial West Village apartments, and active social and romantic lives television had promised them. Instead, skyrocketing rents forced them into outer-borough closets shared with assorted weirdos and an epochal financial crisis left them “funemployed” or hustling. A few years later, TV caught on with a new generation of single-women-in-the-city comedies: Girls, 2 Broke Girls, Broad City. One of the best was also among the least heralded: 2012’s Don’t Trust the B—- in Apartment 23. (Blame the cumbersome title.) Created by Nahnatchka Khan, who would go on to helm the more widely seen sitcom Fresh Off the Boat, the ABC series cast Dreama Walker as wide-eyed Midwesterner June, who moves to Manhattan for a fancy job, only to find the company that hired her in apocalypse mode. Scrambling to salvage the move, she’s bamboozled into sharing an apartment with Chloe (Krysten Ritter), a party-girl con artist and likely sociopath who is always running some deranged scam. Ritter is the main draw here, radiating a reckless charm that makes Chloe lovable even as she does hateful things. Walker’s performance as a basic ingénue whose secret weapon is tenacity makes the roommates perfect foils. Eric André and the late James Van Der Beek round out the dream ensemble as, respectively, June’s coffee-shop boss and—in what might be Van Der Beek’s definitive performance—a vain, sleazy version of himself, still coasting on his Dawson’s Creek fame. The final ingredient is Khan’s particular shade of black humor, synthesizing lightly surreal storylines, twisted one-liners, and an endless supply of deftly deployed cultural references into one of the edgiest shows ever to enter a broadcast primetime schedule.

title: GuliKit’s new Switch controller features next-generation anti-drift thumbsticks
summary: GuliKit announced its first wireless controller to use an improved version of the anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) thumbsticks featured in its budget-friendly ES Pro that debuted nearly a year ago. Available now for $49.99, the new GuliKit ES Max is more expensive than last year's $29.99 ES Pro, but still cheaper than Nintendo's Switch 2 […]
full_text:
GuliKit announced its first wireless controller to use an improved version of the anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) thumbsticks featured in its budget-friendly ES Pro that debuted nearly a year ago. Available now for $49.99, the new GuliKit ES Max is more expensive than last year’s $29.99 ES Pro, but still cheaper than Nintendo’s Switch 2 Pro Controller, while offering more features and functionality without the risk of stick drift that plagued the original Switch.
GuliKit’s new Switch controller features next-generation anti-drift thumbsticks
The ES Max uses a new kind of tunneling magnetoresistance thumbsticks that are more responsive and precise.
The TMR thumbsticks in the ES Max don’t feature a complete reimagining of the technology but measure stick movement in a slightly different way that improves performance. The traditional TMR tech uses a sensor to measure changes in the distance between it and a magnet that moves closer and farther away in response to stick movements.
Instead of measuring changes in the strength of the magnetic field, the new TMR tech uses its sensor to measure the rotational angle of a nearby magnet as it moves along with the stick. With this new approach, the strength of the magnetic field never decreases, resulting in more accurate measurements and thumbsticks that are more precise, responsive, and stable.
The ES Max is compatible with all versions of the Nintendo Switch as well as Windows and macOS PCs, iOS and Android mobile devices, and Steam. Other upgrades include the addition of two remappable buttons on the back, swappable thumbstick caps, and Hall-effect linear triggers that can be switched to micro-switches for shorter travel and faster reactions. GuliKit is also bundling a Hyperlink 2 Bluetooth adapter it claims offers lower latency when using the ES Max as a wireless controller and is introducing its first mobile app for customizing, configuring, and updating its gamepads.

title: Bumble now lets men make the first move
summary: Bumble was famously built around exclusively giving women the power to initiate messages in heterosexual matches when it first launched in 2014 - but now the times they are a-changin' for the dating app. Today, Bumble has announced a "global evolution to its signature conversation experience": anyone can now send the first message, and the […]
full_text:
Bumble was famously built around exclusively giving women the power to initiate messages in heterosexual matches when it first launched in 2014 — but now the times they are a-changin’ for the dating app. Today, Bumble has announced a “global evolution to its signature conversation experience”: anyone can now send the first message, and the deadline to respond before the match expires has been extended from 24 hours to a 72-hour window.
Bumble now lets men make the first move
Message recipients also now have 72 hours to respond instead of just 24 hours.
“While women making the first move was a radical idea, being women-first was never about prescribing just one way to connect. It was about designing an experience with women’s needs in mind to create better outcomes for everyone,” Bumble founder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd said in a statement. “Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides. This evolution isn’t a departure from our founding vision, but the realization of it.”
The change was partially driven by results from user surveys, with Bumble finding that 66 percent of women reported a preference for men to send the first message. During tests, Bumble also reports that opening messages became more evenly distributed between men and women, and chat initiation increased. The changes also aim to address “a growing reality of modern dating,” in which both men and women are busier than ever and the ability to connect with each other is “often lost due to timing, not lack of interest.”
The app is now instead focusing on the quality of those first messages instead of restricting who can send them. “If a member sends a low-effort message, such as a one word opener, they will be prompted to be more thoughtful with their message before they send,” Bumble said in its press release. Bumble released an “Opening Moves” feature two years ago that technically gave men a way to make the first move by responding to prewritten prompts, so this isn’t completely new territory for the dating app. Wolfe Herd first announced this overhaul during Bumble’s latest financial earnings, which reported a continued decline in both revenue and paying users.
Still, that’s a heck of a pivot for the women-first branding that Bumble has built its entire identity around, often being referred to as the “feminist Tinder” of dating apps. A big part of its appeal at launch was enabling women to avoid interacting with creepy men, and the statement on its website once read: “To challenge outdated heterosexual norms, women make the first move on Bumble.”

title: Spotify says it won’t recommend music from ‘AI Personas’
summary: Spotify will soon label AI artists and remove their music from your recommendations. The change, which will start rolling out in mid-September, means you'll see an "AI Persona" badge on an artist's profile across the app if they do "not represent a real person." The music streaming platform will allow artists to disclose that they're […]
full_text:
Spotify will soon label AI artists and remove their music from your recommendations. The change, which will start rolling out in mid-September, means you’ll see an “AI Persona” badge on an artist’s profile across the app if they do “not represent a real person.”
Spotify says it won’t recommend music from ‘AI Personas’
Artist profiles on Spotify that do ‘not represent a real person’ will get an ‘AI Persona’ badge.
The music streaming platform will allow artists to disclose that they’re an AI persona starting today, but it won’t rely solely on self-identification. Spotify says it will use human review and AI tools to determine whether someone’s profile, including their name and image, “appears to represent photorealistic AI-generated identities.” If Spotify determines that an artist’s identity may be AI-generated, it will apply a “Likely AI Persona” badge. Spotify will review artists who meet “defined audience thresholds” first to cover the profiles people listen to the most.
Music from AI personas won’t appear in editorial suggestions or personal recommendations by default. “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated,” Spotify says. “We tune our algorithms to highlight authentic human artists and, based on available signals, strive to not include spam, slop, or low-effort content in our recommendations.”
The move comes as AI music continues to flood streaming platforms, with the music streaming service Deezer recently revealing that AI-generated tracks now make up half of its daily song uploads.
Spotify says its new labels only pertain to an artist’s identity, rather than how they created their music. While Spotify currently doesn’t have a system to identify AI-generated music like Deezer, it allows artists to disclose AI use and launched a “Verified by Spotify” badge to indicate that they’re a real person. The platform will notify artists if it puts a “Likely AI Persona” badge on their profile, and will also give them the ability to appeal. Spotify plans on adding a feature that will let listeners flag artists with potential AI-generated identities as well.

title: Claude will apply invisible watermarks to AI text and images
summary: Anthropic has pledged to start marking Claude-generated text and images with machine-readable data, in an effort to comply with European rules for AI transparency. "Generated text will carry embedded watermarks, and generated files will include digitally signed provenance metadata where supported," Anthropic says on a new Claude support page. The changes are invisible to human […]
full_text:
Anthropic has pledged to start marking Claude-generated text and images with machine-readable data, in an effort to comply with European rules for AI transparency. “Generated text will carry embedded watermarks, and generated files will include digitally signed provenance metadata where supported,” Anthropic says on a new Claude support page. The changes are invisible to human eyes, but will make it easier for people and online platforms to detect if content was generated by Claude models.
Claude will apply invisible watermarks to AI text and images
Anthropic is making its AI-generated content easier to identify, in compliance with EU rules.
These updates are a future commitment rather than something that will go into effect immediately. New AI labeling and transparency obligations under the EU’s AI Act, which came into effect on August 2nd, include a four month compliance grace period for existing AI products that launched prior to that date. As such, Anthropic says new Claude models will mark AI-generated content from day one upon release, but support for its existing models is a work in progress.
The machine-readable marks will be applied globally to supported Claude models, including Claude Platform (API), Claude, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and Claude Tag. Two different marking techniques are being used: For images processed by Claude, C2PA — a provenance metadata standard already embraced by Adobe, OpenAI, and Google — will be applied to supported files, but the process for marking Claude-generated text is much lighter on details.
According to Anthropic, an “imperceptible watermark” is woven directly into the text generated by Claude models without changing the meaning, quality, or readability of the chatbot’s response. Anthropic doesn’t name this watermarking system, but says those text watermarks will also be applied when Claude models are accessed through AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry.
“Because the watermark is part of the text, it will travel with the text when it’s copied and pasted elsewhere, and may persist through some editing,” Anthropic says on the Claude support page. “Watermarking will be applied at the model level, which means it will be present no matter which Claude product or surface the text comes from.”
Anthropic is also working to enable users and other third parties to detect watermarks and provenance metadata embedded into Claude-generated content, and says it’ll share details on this detection system in upcoming technical documentation. There are several tools already available that are designed to detect C2PA metadata, including Google’s Gemini chatbot, but it isn’t clear if those will work with Claude-generated files. I’ve asked Anthropic for clarification.
This is another step toward AI-generated text and images being clearly tagged across online platforms, and a potential win for folks who want to avoid consuming such content. Fanfiction readers have already been building more rudimentary detection systems to flag when Claude tools have been used in AO3 fanworks, but these marking systems can be applied far more broadly — if they work, that is.
C2PA data is known to be easily stripped out, sometimes even accidently when the media carrying it is uploaded to online platforms, and it’s unclear how robust Anthropic’s text watermarking solution is. Even the company itself is hedging that these marking systems are far from infallible, and that any content that lacks detectable marks could still originate from generative AI models.

title: Joby flexes military muscle with $500 million defense acquisition
summary: Joby Aviation announced it was acquiring Dayton, Ohio-based defense firm Resonant Sciences in a $500 million deal, in a bid by the electric aircraft company to expand further into the military industrial complex. Joby says it expects to finance the deal with $450 million in cash and $50 million in equity. After the deal closes, […]
full_text:
Joby Aviation announced it was acquiring Dayton, Ohio-based defense firm Resonant Sciences in a $500 million deal, in a bid by the electric aircraft company to expand further into the military industrial complex.
Joby flexes military muscle with $500 million defense acquisition
The eVTOL company is trying to shore up its defense business with the acquisition of the Dayton, Ohio-based firm.
Joby says it expects to finance the deal with $450 million in cash and $50 million in equity. After the deal closes, which is expected in early 2027, Resonant will continue its existing work as Joby’s dedicated defense division, the company said. The commercial division will remain focused on air taxis, the first of which are expected to launch later this year.
The deal is the latest example of the fledgling electric aviation industry looking beyond urban air taxis for new revenue streams, especially as rising costs and a protracted regulatory approval process pushes air taxi success further into the future. For many, lucrative military contracts represent too ripe an opportunity to pass up.
Resonant Sciences, which was founded in 2015 and employs around 250 people, develops systems that help aircraft see, communicate, and operate in complex environments, including war zones. Its sensors, antennas, and signal-processing technology to gather information support secure communications and protect against interference, while its low-observability expertise helps make aircraft harder to detect. Resonant’s products are already qualified across more than 20 commercial and defense airframes. And many of the firm’s employees have military clearance due to the classified nature of their work.
Joby says the acquisition will allow it to combine its propulsion and autonomy tech with Resonant’s radio frequency, sensing, and mission systems capabilities. The company says it intends to design and build stealth aircraft using its newly acquired systems.
Joby has long had ties to the military, stretching back to 2016 when the company participated in the Department of Defense’s Defense Innovation Unit project. In 2020, Joby became the first eVTOL developer to secure an airworthiness approval and flight clearance certificate from the US Air Force for government-led testing. And in 2023, it delivered its first aircraft to Edwards Air Force Base for testing.
Electric aircraft developers are increasingly looking to military projects to help shore up their cash-intensive business. Air taxis have yet to obtain the necessary government approvals in most markets that would allow them to launch their commercial service and bring in more money. As such, most of these companies, Joby included, regularly report steep quarterly losses. Last week, Joby reported a net loss of $245.4 million in the second quarter of 2026 on $38.6 million in revenue.
Getting more military contracts is increasingly becoming just as important as launching a viable air taxi service. Last month, San Jose-based Archer Aviation, one of Joby’s main rivals, unveiled a new aircraft it codeveloped with defense technology company Anduril. Consolidation is also an emerging theme. Boeing said yesterday it was selling three of its eVTOL subsidiaries to Archer as part of a new blockbuster deal.

title: If crypto goes back to the congressional drawing board, 3 Democrat women loom large
full_text:
If crypto goes back to the congressional drawing board, 3 Democrat women loom large
The Democrats who may get a bigger say in future crypto legislative efforts are familiar figures, and they generally look at digital assets with distrust.
- If the crypto Clarity Act sinks this year, the same four congressional committees that worked on it will be central to whatever happens in the new session of Congress, and odds favor at least two of them being run by Democrats critical of crypto.
- The U.S. House of Representatives is the most likely to flip to Democrat control, which could leave Representative Maxine Waters in charge of the House Financial Services Committee and Shontel Brown running the House Agriculture Committee — both of them with histories opposing crypto bills.
- For the industry, it potentially gets significantly worse if the Senate also changes hands.
Next January, there's a strong chance that U.S. Representative Maxine Waters will steer the destiny of legislation to establish crypto market rules.
The California Democrat stands in line to return to the helm of the House Financial Services Committee, just as a number of other senior Democrats await their potential committee gavels if their party manages to secure majorities in the U.S. House of Representatives or Senate. If Waters takes over her panel, counterpart Representative Shontel Brown could rise to the top of the House Agriculture Committee, the other committee that would likely be in a position to pursue crypto legislation.
If the crypto industry and its congressional allies have to toss the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act in the same bin where they once left its predecessor, the Financial Innovation and Technology for the 21st Century Act (FIT21), potential Democrat committee leaders are unlikely to see crypto regulation occupy the level of priority the current Republicans maintain.
"Regardless of how you feel about crypto, we can't just ignore it," said Blockchain Association CEO Summer Mersinger in a CoinDesk interview. "It's here, and the best thing that we can do is create a federally federal regulatory structure for it. It's hard to argue against that, regardless of whether you like crypto or not."
The betting on Kalshi predicts a Democratic House majority at an 84% likelihood, though that chance is much less (a 47% coin toss) for the Senate, where Democrats face a tougher election battlefield this year. But if they prevail, a Democratic Senate could mean Senator Elizabeth Warren — the bane of crypto lobbyists — ascends to lead the key Senate Banking Committee.
President Donald Trump has made it a special goal to welcome crypto into the U.S. financial regulation tent, with a major win on stablecoins and a contentious fight on market structure. But many of his Democratic political foes have spent considerable time focusing on severing Trump's own crypto business ties. They'll almost certainly pursue congressional investigations of his digital assets activity if they're running the agenda.
Waters has been among the critics of Trump's motives. However, the California lawmaker also had once negotiated an earlier stablecoin effort just inches from the finish line in 2022 — a predecessor to last year's successful Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS) Act. While she's shown a past willingness to take crypto seriously as a topic of legislation, she has been aggressively critical of the Clarity Act (which is facing a narrowing chance for a vote in the Senate).
She called it the "Calamity Act," saying it would "create giant loopholes in our federal financial laws that would put consumers and investors at risk," and it would handcuff the regulators policing the sector. Waters also staged a walk-out of a Clarity hearing in her committee.
She also recently opposed crypto in people's retirement accounts and, last year, pushed one of several bills targeting Trump's crypto empire.
If Waters focused on countering Trump's crypto activity in a return as chairwoman, even a legislative win probably wouldn't negate the president's potential conflicts of interest, because he'd be in a position to veto it. Her office didn’t respond to a request for comment on her plans.
The House and Senate each have a pair of committees that are most centrally engaged on crypto policy, thanks to the U.S.'s unusual split of regulation between separate agencies that concentrate on securities (the Securities and Exchange Commission) and derivatives (the Commodity Futures Trading Commission). So, the agriculture committees in both chambers oversee the CFTC, and the SEC is under the jurisdiction of the Senate Banking committee and House Financial Services Committee.
Shontel Brown is a strong possibility to lead the House Agriculture Committee if Democrats secure the majority, and that's another potential problem for crypto. The Ohio Democrat has opposed all digital assets bills in the past, up to the Clarity Act, earning an "F" grade from crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto. However, she said she could get behind crypto policy that "protects consumers and allows innovation to benefit everyone."
"I voted against the GENIUS and Clarity acts because they fail to adequately address abuse and instead open the door to corruption," she said last year. "At a time when the current occupant of the Oval Office is personally benefiting from crypto and memecoin ventures, these bills do nothing to close conflict-of-interest loopholes."
But if Waters and Brown are running the crypto show in the House, the White House will still have its same occupant. Even if the Democrats win a stronger majority than the narrow GOP advantage of the past two years, the next session could become a mess of go-nowhere, message-sending bills. If the party won the Senate majority, too, that wouldn't help assure Democrats an ability to get legislation converted to law.
On the Senate side, Senator Warren has been among the crypto industry's most prominent Capitol Hill detractors, trying to keep a steady spotlight on what she's portrayed as the president's crypto corruption. However, under her time as the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, she watched her fellow Democrats go against her on crypto matters, gathering for negotiations on the legislation she opposed.
She may have more sway were she to lead the committee and control the advancement of her members' bills. If she were to follow in the footsteps of the most recent Democrat who ran the banking panel, former Senator Sherrod Brown, she could go for years without allowing a crypto measure through the gate. (Brown, who was defeated by Republican crypto advocate Senator Bernie Moreno two years ago with the help of a massive $40 million crypto PAC boost, is also running again for the other Ohio Senate seat.)
On the Senate Agriculture committee, Senator Amy Klobuchar has been the top Democrat, but there's a strong chance she's heading toward the Minnesota governor's mansion this year. That would leave Senator Michael Bennet of Colorado next in line of seniority, since he fell short in his own governor bid when he lost in his state's June primary.
Bennet has voted against crypto policies at every turn, and he introduced a bill in May that would have imposed crypto bans on government officials — including the president — in language much stronger than the compromise effort that was in the Clarity Act.
All four of these leading Democrats in the relevant committees — Waters, Brown, Warren and Bennet — have matching "F" ratings from Stand With Crypto. So if the Clarity Act fails to advance during its brief Senate window in September, it's likely that the crypto industry would be facing significant headwinds when it tries again.
Still, Digital Chamber CEO Cody Carbone, whose Washington group has been among those trying to push the legislation through Congress, argued that crypto should still be considered "non-partisan."

title: Crypto-friendly bank Erebor in talks to raise $1.5 billion at $9.5 billion valuation: FT
full_text:
Crypto-friendly bank Erebor in talks to raise $1.5 billion at $9.5 billion valuation: FT
Total deposits grew from $1.1 billion in March to $4.6 billion by July, driven by clients in crypto, AI and defense.
- Erebor Bank is negotiating a $1.5 billion funding round for a total valuation of $9.5 billion, according to the Financial Times.
- The capital infusion is designed to meet a mandatory 12% leverage ratio while it expands lending operations, including a $200 million facility for Valar Atomics.
- Total deposits grew from $1.1 billion in March to $4.6 billion by July, driven by clients in crypto, AI and defense.
Tech-oriented lender Erebor Bank is in advanced talks to raise about $1.5 billion in a deal that would value the year-old firm at about $9.5 billion, the Financial Times reported.
Lux Capital, Human Capital, Valor Equity Partners, Andreessen Horowitz and SV Angel are expected to make large commitments in the fundraising round. Existing investors including 8VC and Haun Ventures are also set to take part, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter.
The fundraising comes as Erebor expands its deposit base and starts lending activity. Deposits reached $4.6 billion by the end of July, up from $1.1 billion at the end of March, the FT said.
Erebor targets companies working in crypto, artificial intelligence, defense and manufacturing. It also serves payment companies, investment funds and trading firms and its planned services include deposits, credit, stablecoin products, treasury management and payments.
The bank received final U.S. approval to operate in February. Regulators require it to maintain a leverage ratio of at least 12% during its first three years, making the fresh capital important as its balance sheet grows.
The bank’s lending push includes a $200 million credit facility for nuclear start-up Valar Atomics. Valar said earlier this month that Erebor led the facility as administrative agent, working with JPMorgan, Crescent Cove and Hercules Capital.
The FT said Erebor raised money earlier this year at a $4.35 billion valuation, meaning the proposed round would nearly double its private-market value in months.

title: Pokémon cards are becoming multibillion dollar market. Crypto wants to fix how they trade
full_text:
Pokémon cards are becoming multibillion dollar market. Crypto wants to fix how they trade
Collectors are spending millions on trading cards, while blockchain startups are turning physical Pokémon cards into digital assets. The harder task is creating enough liquidity to compete with established marketplaces.
- A booming Pokémon trading card market, now estimated at roughly $10 billion to $15 billion, has driven long lines at retailers like Costco and record-breaking sales, including Logan Paul’s $16.5 million Pikachu Illustrator card.
- Big-box chains such as Target and Walmart, along with eBay’s $2.62 billion in 2025 card sales, highlight how trading cards have evolved into a major alternative asset class that has recently outperformed the S&P 500 and bitcoin.
- Startups like ATH Labs’ Deadstock are betting that tokenizing high-grade cards on blockchains and storing them in vaults can modernize this fragmented, slow-to-trade market, though they still face stiff liquidity and network-effect advantages from incumbents like eBay.
It’s 3:30 a.m. on a cool April morning, and hundreds of people are already lined up outside a Costco in British Columbia, some sitting in folding chairs, hours before the store opens.
The buyers aren't here for a bulk deal on toilet paper or groceries. They’re waiting to be the first to get their hands on boxes of Pokémon cards, specifically the "Prismatic Evolutions" cards, selling around C$100 each. On secondary marketplaces such as Facebook Marketplace, the cards often get listed for several times their retail price.
And just recently, popular influencer Logan Paul sold a rare Pokémon card, a Pikachu Illustrator, for $16.5 million dollars, reportedly earning him more than $8 million in profit. The buyer? AJ Scaramucci, founder of venture capital firm Solari Capital and son of financier Anthony Scaramucci.
In addition to Costco, other big-box retailers are seeing the Pokémon card frenzy show up in their businesses. Target said that sales of its trading cards were up nearly 70% last year, driven largely by Pokémon, and that it plans to expand store space dedicated to trading cards as part of its growth strategy. Walmart also reported its online marketplace saw 200% jump in trading card sales last year. Both retailers have had to impose purchase limits on trading cards to curb scalping. Meanwhile, eBay, the largest marketplace for these cards, saw $2.62 billion in sales in 2025.
In fact, both the S&P 500 (up about 13%) and bitcoin (down 29%) underperformed this year compared with the value of Pokémon cards (rose 28%).
The hype is part of a broader transformation of trading cards from hobby-store collectibles into a multibillion-dollar market that increasingly resembles an alternative asset class.
Exactly how large this market is hard to pin down, because it has developed through dense, decentralized dealer networks, local card shops and conventions. So the market size varies by methodology and firm, but the rough estimates put the value around $10-$15 billion today. For example, Kovoy VC, which invests in gaming platforms and tech, pegged the value at around $13 billion in 2024, and Mordor Intelligence puts it at around $15 billion in 2026. Meanwhile, TCGCharts estimates that the market cap of every "graded" card is around $10.8 billion today.
But there’s a big problem: the trading card business is booming, but the infrastructure required to trade them quickly and efficiently hasn’t kept pace with the explosion of popularity.
Collectors are still stuck with a 1990s-style slow, arduous process of waiting weeks or months for their cards to be graded for value, listing them on inefficient marketplaces with high fees, and then having to ship them by snail mail to reach buyers. For the new generation of investors, who are used to transacting financial assets within a fraction of a second, the process seems antiquated.
Blockchain solution
A new class of platforms is betting that blockchain technology can replace some of those old ways by storing the physical card in a secure vault while enabling faster, digital ownership transfers.
One of such products is Deadstock, the first platform from startup ATH Labs. The firm, based in Abu Dhabi and co-founded by Dominic Jang, a longtime Pokémon card collector and traditional finance veteran, runs a closed beta of its platform on the Arbitrum blockchain, featuring high-value, professionally graded Pokémon cards. Bullish Capital, CoinDesk’s parent company’s venture arm, has invested in the company.
ATH is betting that the next stage of growth in the collectibles market will depend less on creating more cards than on making existing ones easier to trade, finance and use as collateral.
"There has never been a central registry or clearing house for this market," ATH argued in a recent research report. That fragmentation, the firm said, creates an opportunity for blockchain-based ownership and settlement infrastructure.
The company is aiming to do so by placing physical cards, primarily ‘PSA-10s’ (cards receiving the highest grade awarded by Professional Sports Authenticator), in a secure, professionally managed vault. Each physical card would then be matched one-to-one with a digital token representing ownership. The token could change hands while the underlying card remains in storage, only moving when an owner chooses to redeem it for physical delivery.
The process is similar to putting physical assets, such as gold, Treasury bills, stocks and private credit, onto the blockchain. This process, called tokenization, has become one of the biggest topics in blockchain technology recently, as proponents say it reduces costs, makes settlement more efficient and enables around-the-clock trading of assets.
That model, for trading cards, appears to be attracting user activity.
Courtyard, one of the best-known platforms in the trading card space, offers digital packs whose contents correspond to physical collectibles held in a vault. It currently processes roughly $139 million of volume over 30 days and is running at an annualized fee of about $48 million, according to DeFiLlama data.
There are other blockchain platforms tokenizing trading cards, including Collector-Crypto ($148.2 million in annualized fees and $77.8 million in 30-day volume) and Phygitals ($15.2 million in annualized fees and $7.4 million in 30-day volume).
The growth of Courtyard and other platforms provides early evidence of demand to trade vaulted physical collectibles on crypto rails.
“For years, we tried to make RWAs work. we got stuff like tokenized credit facilities for shoddy motorcycle loans in east africa. turns out people just wanted tokenized psa 10 first edition shadowless charizards,” said VC firm Paradigm’s general partner, who goes by “Frankie,” in an X post.
However, their volumes remain small compared to the incumbent marketplaces that dominate card trading. The composition of these activities also warrants some caution, according to House of Chimera, a crypto research firm. The firm found that much of the volume comes from gamified pack openings and instant buybacks rather than collectors simply buying and selling individual cards with one another.
Additionally, Asia-based MemeStrategy has also entered the market, claiming to have launched the “world’s first” tokenized Pokémon trading card fund, designed to offer professional investors access to PSA-10-graded "Pikachu with Grey Felt Hat" trading cards available on the market.
ATH is trying to differentiate itself by focusing on a different part of the market: access to supply. "We aren't just tokenizing a card, we are tokenizing a lot of cards," said Jang.
House of Chimera found that many tokenized-card platforms rely on the same grading and storage providers, making the underlying infrastructure relatively similar across competitors. The research firm said a more meaningful advantage may be having enough capital and inventory to support buybacks and liquidity.

title: ADI Chain, Shipfinex partner to tokenize $500M vessel pipeline
summary: Shipfinex plans to bring 35 vessels onchain through ADI Chain as tokenization expands into the multitrillion-dollar maritime industry.
full_text:
ADI Chain, Shipfinex partner to tokenize $500M vessel pipeline
Shipfinex plans to bring 35 vessels onchain through ADI Chain as tokenization expands into the multitrillion-dollar maritime industry.
Dubai-based maritime asset tokenization platform Shipfinex partnered with ADI Chain to tokenize a pipeline of around 35 vessels worth $500 million, as it looks to open new financing channels for shipowners.
According to the company, the vessels will be placed in separate special-purpose vehicles, with the resulting tokens potentially representing vessel-backed credit, charter-linked income or other economic interests in individual ships.
ADI Chain, an Abu Dhabi-based blockchain focused on stablecoins and real-world assets, will provide the distribution and settlement infrastructure. Primary allocations and distributions are expected to use UAE dirham-, US dollar- and other currency-denominated stablecoins.
The planned tokenization represents a small share of the broader shipping market. The world fleet and orderbook were valued at about $2.1 trillion at the start of 2026, according to Clarksons Research data.
The partnership is still in the pilot and operational-readiness stage, with no Maritime Asset Tokens publicly issued and the regulated issuance route still being finalized.
The deal comes as the market for tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) continues to grow. Assets tracked by RWA.xyz totaled about $38.1 billion as of Aug. 9, led by $16.2 billion in US Treasury debt and $4.9 billion in commodities.
In a report released Monday, Standard Chartered forecast that tokenized RWAs could reach $4 trillion by the end of 2028, according to Geoff Kendrick, the bank’s global head of digital asset research.
