- list 2 of 3Police arrest dozens at London rally supporting Palestine Action
- list 3 of 3UK left-wing MP Diane Abbott reinstated by Labour Party after suspension
Prison services are devolved in Scotland and Northern Ireland, but are still centrally controlled in England and Wales.
Here is what we know about the row and why England and Wales are facing a prisons crisis.
What has Burnham said about prisons since taking over as prime minister?
Burnham, who took over as prime minister last month after Starmer’s ousting just two years after winning a landslide election, paused the early release scheme for review following public backlash over the news that some rapists and child-grooming convicts might be freed. The family of slain PC Andrew Harper, who was killed in 2019, also protested.
Harper died after being dragged by a car driven by the two killers who were escaping from a burglary. They were convicted of manslaughter.
Following this review, Burnham said on August 4 that the Sentencing Act would no longer apply to those guilty of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences. That brought the number of inmates eligible for early release to around 5,000, rather than the previously estimated 6,000. However, the exemptions do not include those convicted of manslaughter, as well as other charges.
Burnham has also moved the start date for the scheme back by one month to October, and has announced extra supervision of those released and more support for victims.
Adding the crime of manslaughter to the list of exclusions to prevent the release of PC Harper’s killers would result in blocking the early release of around 1,000 inmates, according to estimates published by British media.
While there have been calls to add manslaughter of an emergency worker as an exception, this is not a specific offence, and the government has said that such an amendment would not be legally feasible.
Experts say the British prison system is on the verge of collapse, as it has one of the highest imprisonment rates in Western Europe, and successive governments have grappled with unpopular options to solve the emergency.
Burnham has vowed to take concerns on board, but ultimately, he said he would see the policy through. “I am doing all I can,” he wrote on X. “But it is simply not possible to prevent all offenders from being released early without the prison system collapsing.”
What happened to PC Andrew Harper?
Twenty-eight-year-old PC Harper from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, was killed in 2019, just four weeks after getting married, as he responded to reports of a burglary. As three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire, his ankle became caught in the getaway car’s tow-rope loop, and he was dragged along a country road for more than a mile (1.8km), suffering fatal injuries.
Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, two of his killers who were convicted of manslaughter, were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020. Under usual rules, they would have to serve at least two-thirds of their sentences before they could be considered for release.
Under the new scheme, however, they would be eligible for release in June 2027, just halfway through their sentences.
A third killer, Henry Long, was given a longer sentence, which requires his case to be seen by the Parole Board before any release can be granted.
The police officer’s widow, Lissie Harper, has pleaded for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release. Chris Bushnell, a former police dog handler who was at the scene of PC Harper’s death, told media in the United Kingdom that he was “shaking” when he was informed that the officer’s killers might be eligible under the scheme.
Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC she was in “turmoil” over the conflicting reports that Cole and Bowers could be eligible for release next year.
Some 900,000 people have signed a petition to prevent the killers’ early release. On Wednesday, 50 police chiefs also signed a letter urging Burnham to pursue every legal option to prevent their release.
How has PM Burnham responded to this case?
Andy Burnham is under increasing pressure to block the release of the killers of PC Harper, and is reportedly actively seeking ways to be able to do this.
On social media, the prime minister said he fully appreciated the “anguish” felt by Harper’s family and said the scheme could be mitigated by expanding prison places in other ways, including removing foreign offenders more quickly and repurposing some women’s prisons for male offenders.
“However, I recognise that, even with all these changes, there will be concerns from many victims about who will still be released early for other offences,” Burnham said on Tuesday.
He added that he was “confident” that the release of the most serious offenders, including Harper’s killers, could be prevented. However, it remains unclear how he intends to do that.
Why is there a prisons crisis in the UK?
Britain’s prisons are nearing the breaking point, experts say, while the prison population is projected to keep rising.
According to the Institute for Government, an independent British think tank, the prison population has doubled over the past 30 years despite falling crime rates. This is largely due to longer sentences being passed and a growing number of people being recalled to prison following release.
As a result, men’s prisons are currently 97 percent full, according to the think tank. Building new prisons would not solve the problem in time, given that it can take an average of seven years to construct and open a new, operational facility, with projects often suffering delays. Additionally, lack of adequate staffing is a long-running problem for British jails.
The think tank said public campaigns calling for the creation of new offences or the introduction of longer sentences have also contributed to the overcrowding.
In 2020, the Conservative government led by Prime Minister Boris Johnson increased the length of sentences for certain serious offences by one-third, while in 2022, the Conservative government of PM Rishi Sunak did the same for a wider group of offences, despite there not being enough capacity in prisons to absorb the increase.
According to independent UK charity Prison Reform Trust, years of rising sentence lengths have driven the prison population close to the limits of available capacity.
“The current crisis is the result of successive governments relying increasingly on imprisonment, while population growth has outpaced the construction of new prison places,” Alex Hewson, the charity’s senior policy and communications officer, told Al Jazeera.
Research conducted by the organisation found that between 2024 and 2025, almost three-quarters of prisons (72 percent) in England and Wales were overcrowded. More than 21,600 people – one-quarter of the prison population – were being held in overcrowded accommodation.

title: Iran is not anti-imperialist. It is a state calculating survival
summary: Regardless of its current hostile rhetoric, the Islamic Republic will likely reach a settlement with the US and Israel.
full_text:
Iran is not anti-imperialist. It is a state calculating survival
Regardless of its current hostile rhetoric, the Islamic Republic will likely reach a settlement with the US and Israel.
More than five months into the US-Israel war on Iran, the prospects for a deal that would end the confrontation remain unclear. Earlier this week, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were no direct negotiations with the United States.
Meanwhile, hostile rhetoric and calls for revenge continue to emanate from Tehran. Some Western commentators, especially on the right, have claimed that Iran is incapable of striking a deal because of its anti-American ideology. But that is a flawed assumption.
One just needs to look at the Iranian constitution and its recent history to discover that the Islamic Republic is not governed solely by ideology. The regime, in its present form, would not shy away from reaching a settlement with the US and even Israel, if it fell in line with its guiding principle: regime survival.
The limits of Iranian anti-imperialism
In January 1988, Iranian Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini settled an internal dispute over the scope of velayat-e faqih, the guardianship of the Islamic jurist, by declaring that the Islamic government ranks above all other rulings of Islam, including prayer, fasting and pilgrimage. The following month, he ordered the creation of a body to resolve deadlocks between the parliament and the Guardian Council by determining what was in the interest of the governing system.
The revisions to the constitution in 1989 gave it a permanent place as Article 112: the Council for Discerning the Expediency of the System.
The message was explicit. Preservation of the system — hefz-e nezam — was the highest religious obligation, and an organ was established to license departures from religious law whenever the system required them.
In the following years, this principle was clearly applied in how the Islamic Republic deployed official ideology, including its hostility towards Washington and Tel Aviv.
Today Tehran presents its anti-imperialist doctrine as a moral commitment grounded in opposition to domination, colonialism and Western hegemony. That self-presentation has earned it sympathy well beyond its borders, including among people who acknowledge its repression at home while treating it as an indispensable pillar of resistance abroad.
But Iran’s anti-imperialism is positional rather than universal. It opposes domination when the Islamic Republic is the object of it, but it has not consistently opposed domination as a political relationship.
The doctrine of “forward defence” has often treated Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Palestine as arenas in which Tehran deters enemies, projects power and acquires leverage. The anti-imperialist principle is therefore applied selectively.
Iran invokes sovereignty and self-determination when resisting external interference in its own affairs, while its regional strategy has often compromised those same principles elsewhere by subordinating other societies to its own security interests.
This behaviour is not peculiar to Iran, nor does it make Iran uniquely cynical. Realist theory has long held that survival is the primary end of states, from which other objectives are derived. On that reading, Iran is not an aberration. It is an ordinary state with an unusually elaborate justificatory apparatus.
That is exactly the point, and it is what makes a bargain thinkable.
The Islamic Republic’s commitments operate on two levels. Enmity towards the US and Israel, support for allied movements and the rejection of accommodation all guide policy. Above them sits a second-order norm that determines when the first-order commitments may be revised. That norm is hefz-e nezam, and Article 112 is its institutional expression.
Survival is the core; anti-imperialism is the protective belt, and belts can be loosened.
A settlement with the enemy
The Islamic Republic speaks the language of principle honoured regardless of cost while governing by calculation of consequence. That gap is not hypocrisy so much as a structural feature of any state that rules in a doctrine’s name, but it leaves a standing problem. It must compromise without appearing to have compromised.
The record shows how this is possible. In July 1988, Khomeini accepted the ceasefire with Iraq, saying publicly that doing so was more lethal to him than poison.
During that war, with the immediate danger coming from Saddam Hussein rather than the “Great Satan”, Tehran accepted American weapons routed through Israeli channels and entered secret dealings with Washington in what eventually would be known as the Iran-Contra affair. After the 9/11 attacks and the US invasion of Afghanistan, Iranian and American diplomats cooperated at the Bonn conference to shape the post-Taliban government.
None of this made Iran pro-American or pro-Israeli, and none of it shows that its doctrine was decorative. It shows that apparently absolute prohibitions have an off-switch, and that the switch is labelled survival.
This year the mechanism has operated under far greater strain. Strikes by the US and Israel on February 28 killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on the first day of a war whose declared aims included forcing regime change in Tehran. Within days, the Assembly of Experts for Leadership installed his son Mojtaba in a hereditary succession that the republic’s own doctrine disparages — another first-order norm surrendered to protect the core.
On June 17, President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU), which included an end to hostilities, sanctions relief, access to frozen funds and reconstruction support. Mojtaba Khamenei endorsed it in writing while recording his misgivings. Again, the core held, but the belt was loosened.
The memorandum left much unresolved, and renewed fighting exposed its fragility. But its existence remains significant. Under existential pressure, the Islamic Republic accepted direct arrangements with Washington and made confrontation itself negotiable.
How can a state enter such an arrangement without renouncing the identity that legitimises it? Not by announcing that anti-imperialism has been abandoned, but by revising what it means. Ali Khamenei supplied the vocabulary in 2013 when he spoke of “heroic flexibility”, invoking a wrestler who gives ground without forgetting his opponent’s capabilities. Concession becomes strategic patience, and retreat becomes the preservation of the struggle.
Supporters largely follow, and not out of confusion. Where an institution interprets its own doctrine, that doctrine cannot constrain it, and a follower who defers to the leader’s reading is applying the principle as the system defines it. So the leadership can cross its own red line without losing its base, because much of the base crosses along with it.
The MoU follows the same logic. Anti-imperialism was not abandoned but reinterpreted as preserving Iran’s capacity to resist under changed conditions.
The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action signed in 2015 had already framed negotiation not as surrender but as another means of defending Iran’s interests. The same logic could support a future settlement involving the US and, indirectly, Israel, without recognition or reconciliation, if mutual restraint is judged better for the system’s survival than continued confrontation.
An agreement with the enemy reduces the risk of war and eases economic strangulation, both of which matter enormously to ordinary Iranians. But relief abroad does not mechanically produce liberty at home.
The state has already invoked wartime conditions to expand arrests, expedite prosecutions and accelerate executions. That repressive apparatus was not built by sanctions and will not be dismantled by their removal. Sanctions relief may ease hardship for Iranians, but without political reform it could also leave the state with greater resources to sus

title: Argentina star Messi not certain to play ‘much longer’ after father’s death
summary: Former Barcelona and PSG star Lionel Messi, who won the 2022 World Cup, hints at retirement from football.
full_text:
Argentina star Messi not certain to play ‘much longer’ after father’s death
Former Barcelona and PSG star Lionel Messi, who won World Cup 2022, hints at retirement.
Argentina superstar Lionel Messi, one of the greatest footballers to play the game, has hinted that he may soon retire from the sport after the death of his father.
The 39-year-old, who was part of the Argentina side that was defeated by Spain in the FIFA World Cup 2026 final, rose to the top of the game from the youth ranks at Spanish club Barcelona.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Poland says Women’s World Cup plan on course despite UEFA boycott of FIFA
- list 2 of 4Trump says ousting FIFA boss Infantino would be ‘terrible’ mistake
- list 3 of 4‘Football belongs to no individual’: UEFA, AFC and CONCACAF slam Infantino
- list 4 of 4FIFA decries ‘concerted’ effort to undermine Infantino as crisis deepens
After his country’s loss to Spain in July in New Jersey at the World Cup, Messi returned to play domestic football in the United States with Major League Soccer (MLS) side Inter Miami.
The forward was forced to cut short his return after the death of his father, Jorge Messi, at the age of 68 this past weekend, and he announced on Wednesday that his playing days may now be coming to an end.
“All I ever did was play football, and now I have serious doubts about whether I’ll keep doing it for much longer,” Messi posted on the social media platform Instagram.
“I don’t know what I’m going to do without you. I don’t know how to carry on.
“You were by my side from the very beginning; there was so little left until the end. Why couldn’t you hold on just a little longer so we could finish it together?”
Messi, whose father was also his agent, is still under contract with Miami until the end of the 2028 season, but following Argentina’s failure to defend the title they won at Qatar 2022 – Messi’s first World Cup trophy – it was rumoured the forward may soon hang up his boots.
In his message, the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star also reflected on the final months of his father’s life, which coincided with the World Cup.
“I kept telling you we would reach the final so you could make the trip,” said Messi, who returned to the US on Tuesday night following his father’s funeral on Sunday.
“We made it to the final, but you couldn’t be there. I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn’t, my legs just gave out.
“This time I tried to push past my physical limits, but I couldn’t. I never felt right,” Messi said in his first comments after the 1-0 defeat by Spain.
Messi also highlighted his father’s pivotal role in his life and career: “You were a father, a friend, and an agent. You were always exactly who you needed to be in every moment, and you never put a foot wrong.”
Jorge Messi’s unusual absence from the World Cup in June had already attracted attention.
Messi’s family asked the media for “humanity” during the tournament amid persistent rumours over Jorge’s health.
After bursting into tears after scoring against Algeria in a group match, Messi had admitted to dealing with “a situation outside of sports”.
Messi, who was his country’s captain at the World Cup, also revealed that one of the main reasons he appeared at the last edition was because it was his father’s wish.
“You always asked me to play in the last World Cup and a few days before it started was when you got worse,” Messi said.
“It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament … Every time a match ended, I would wait and hope for your message. That’s when I realised how real the situation was.”
On Sunday, the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner bid farewell to his father during a private ceremony with close family and a few Argentina teammates in the town of Perez, adjacent to Rosario.
The cause of death was not disclosed, but local media reported that Jorge Messi had been suffering from cancer.
Despite his grief, Messi pledged to honour his father’s memory through parenting his own children.
“I’m going to miss you so much, but you will always be present, especially in the upbringing of my children, because I will teach them and raise them the way you raised me,” he said.

title: ‘Burn in hell’: Israeli settlers spread hate through graffiti, attacks
summary: Racist settler graffiti on West Bank homes and schools reveals a brazen ideological drive for Palestinian displacement.
full_text:
‘Burn in hell’: Israeli settlers spread hate through graffiti, attacks
Walls across occupied West Bank have been transformed into canvases for racist slogans, signaling a brazen drive for displacement of Palestinians.
Scrawled in black graffiti, the word “Revenge” stains the terracotta facade of a school in Jalud, a village in the occupied West Bank.
Other slogans carry a more direct threat: “Burn in hell,” reads one. “Get out of the village,” says another.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli government accused of complicity as settlers demolish Jericho homes
- list 2 of 3Israeli raids, arrests continue as UN warns West Bank at ‘breaking point’
- list 3 of 3Palestine weekly: Netanyahu hedges on Gaza roadmap
It is a familiar sight across this community, located 27km (17 miles) south of Nablus and home to some 1,000 Palestinians.
Under the cover of darkness or in broad daylight, Israeli settlers have been targeting Palestinian public institutions and homes with increased intensity, spraying slogans with racist and threatening messages, as well as invoking biblical passages to justify committing their crimes.
Residents and officials say the defacing of the buildings typically accompanies violent settler attacks. Jalud has been subjected to five major assaults since last January, the latest being on August 4 when settlers burned vehicles and sprayed racist slogans on a residential building.
‘Take revenge here’
Jalud resident Misbah al-Haj Mohammed said some of the slogans bear the names of settlers who carried out previous attacks, as if wanting to “challenge” people in the village and neighbouring areas.
He added that the messages written on school walls are aimed specifically at children to create a sense of fear in them about attending classes, while those threatening expulsion want to signify that “killing and displacement are inevitably coming”.
The head of the village council, Raed al-Haj Mohammed, described the slogans as “racist and liquidationist”, saying they are usually used by members of the Hilltop Youth group calling for the expulsion of Palestinians.
A decentralised network made up mostly of Jewish youths between the ages of 15 and 20, the Hilltop Youth is among the most prominent violent settler groups in the West Bank.
The group takes its name from a strategy of establishing settlement outposts on “hilltops”, a term referring not only to the land itself, but also to a settlement model based on creating new outposts outside existing illegal settlements and later imposing a fait accompli to pave the way for their legalisation.
“When a soldier is killed in Gaza, they take revenge here, and write the names of their dead on our walls,” Raed told Al Jazeera, adding that residents immediately move to remove the slogans.
‘Zero-Arab state’
Azzam Abu al-Adas, a researcher in Israeli affairs, said the settlers’ choice of writings was a “reflection of deep ideological concepts”.
He cited the slogan “Death to Arabs”, describing it as “an explicit call for genocide, within a replacement settlement vision seeking to reach a zero-Arab state in the region extending between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea”.
Abu al-Adas pointed out that the idea of genocide has become a “mainstream current” in Israeli society since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023, entrenching a conviction that solving the “Palestinian problem” could only happen through “annihilating Palestinians or expelling them permanently, and destroying the urban environment they inhabit to get rid of their presence completely”.
Referring to The Price Tag movement, a clandestine network of far-right settler groups that emerged in 2008, Abu al-Aldas said that from an ideological perspective, its members see Palestinians as the “occupier” of the land who must pay the price for their stay until they are “forced to leave and exit … permanently”.
He added that the scrawled slogans often include the names of killed settlers, meant to signal that the attack was a “retaliatory act for their memory” and pointed to an escalation in the use of religious texts employed to incite the killing of non-Jews, alongside slogans about “the promise of the Lord”.
Walid Habbas, a researcher in Israeli affairs, said the violent settler groups “want to punish the Palestinian existence itself because it obstructs the project of controlling the land and not only because it carried out resistance”.
Habbas said that burning crops, mosques and homes “is not a random choice” as it targets the elements of survival and connection to the place.
Habbas also noted that some of the messages, which are written in Hebrew, are not primarily directed at Palestinians, who may not read the language. Instead, they serve as an “ownership mark” addressing other settlers, as well as the Israeli state and public. Consequently, “the Palestinian wall turns into a banner declaring that the place has become, symbolically, a reclaimed land”, said Habbas.
He added that the writing of such slogans aims to strip Palestinians of their humanity and make harming them acceptable, as well as providing “holy cover” to perpetrators and entrenching the argument that the land “does not accommodate two peoples”.
Habbas cited an attack last month on the village of Qusra, where settlers set fire to a mosque and sprayed slogans and a Star of David on its walls. The targeting of the mosque “is not a revenge against an individual, but a strike at the unifying structure that produces collective identity and connection to the place”, he said.
The Star of David serves as a “sovereign signature”, saying that “this place is subject to us”, added Habbas.
He also highlighted what he believes is the attack’s most dangerous aspect: the writing is “crude, fast and unhidden”, drawn on a facade overlooking the public road so it is seen and photographed.
He described this deliberate act as “not recklessness”, but a “declaration of confidence that the perpetrator will not be held accountable”, and that “the public nature of the crime itself is a message about the balance of power and a structural complicity that makes this violence possible and recurrent”.

title: How Africa is becoming a ‘strategic hub’ for Chinese industrial expansion
summary:
For decades, resource-rich African nations operated on a straightforward pit-to-ship model whereby foreign operators extracted raw ore, loaded it onto cargo ships and exported it abroad, leaving producer countries with little to show for it.
Today, nations such as Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Ghana and Guinea are dismantling that system – by banning exports of raw materials and enforcing local processing rules. These measures force international mining firms, including Chinese companies, to...
full_text:
How Africa is becoming a ‘strategic hub’ for Chinese industrial expansion
Countries including Zimbabwe and Guinea are ending the pit-to-ship model that saw them exporting raw minerals with limited local gains
Today, nations such as Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Ghana and Guinea are dismantling that system – by banning exports of raw materials and enforcing local processing rules. These measures force international mining firms, including Chinese companies, to invest billions of dollars in domestic processing plants.
Now, instead of simply shipping out ore, Chinese firms are building local facilities to transform Zimbabwean lithium into its sulphate or carbonate forms, Guinean bauxite into alumina, and Mozambican graphite into battery materials.
According to Carlos Lopes, a professor at the University of Cape Town’s Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance, the shift runs far deeper than resource processing. “China increasingly sees Africa as one of the few remaining large-scale spaces where industrial expansion, urbanisation, infrastructure deployment and consumer growth can still unfold simultaneously over decades,” he said.
The continent was becoming less a peripheral supplier and more a strategic hub between fractured economic blocs, Lopes said, with Chinese firms more likely to localise where governments ensured policy clarity, reliable energy, domestic demand and regional scale.
“Bans on unprocessed exports will not necessarily deter investment,” he said, adding that the African countries imposing the bans could actually improve investment quality by forcing longer-term commitments.
However, these policies were only successful when states possessed negotiating discipline and institutional coherence, Lopes warned – otherwise, bans risked becoming blunt instruments that fuelled smuggling, policy volatility and elite rent-seeking.

summary:

The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Canadian airline WestJet has agreed to pay C$4.5m (£2.4m) to settle a decade-long sexual harassment class action lawsuit levelled by its female flight attendants, who alleged the company failed to maintain a safe workplace.
The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk.
A British Columbia judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalised on 22 June after months of negotiation. The payment will be distributed among the 3,452 flight attendants in the class action after expenses are removed, including legal fees.
WestJet agreed to hire a third-party to conduct a workplace inquiry that will examine the prevalence of harassment, the extent of underreporting and how reporting systems can be made more effective.
The suit had called on WestJet to implement mandatory anti-harassment training for pilots, along with an admission of wrongdoing and an admission of a breach of employee contract. None were included in the settlement.
Lewis filed the initial class action against the airline in April 2016. She said she was dismayed by the results, especially given that two years ago WestJet paid out $12.5m in a baggage fee class action, nearly three times the amount agreed to in the sexual harassment suit.
“I’m glad it’s over … but I’m just exhausted. I’m shaking my head,” she said, adding that she was advised the amount was the most that could be achieved given that legal expenses were piling up.
Under BC law, the suit included all female flight attendants who worked for the company between 4 April 2014 and 28 February 2021, because Lewis’s suit alleged that all of them had their contracts violated by WestJet during that period because its employee policy promised that the workplace would be free from harassment. The suit claimed WestJet broke its policy by not taking enough steps to address reports of assault or to prevent harassment in the first place.
Lewis said she was sexually assaulted by a WestJet pilot while on a layover in Hawaii in 2010 when she was 25 years old. In court documents, she said the same pilot had also assaulted another flight attendant in 2008.
Though she reported the assault to WestJet, the pilot remained at the company and Lewis was eventually fired in 2016 for “gross insubordination”, according to court documents submitted by WestJet that year, which she and her legal team allege was retaliation for trying to hold the airline accountable internally. She said she abandoned an individual civil claim and instead created the class action after learning other flight attendants had also experienced harassment.
Lewis said she reported the assault to police in Maui but alleges WestJet rerouted the pilot so he would not face questioning in Hawaii.
She said fellow members of the class action suit were also disappointed with the result. Eight of them had already asked the province’s supreme court not to approve the settlement in February when some of the details first emerged, citing a low payout and a lack of accountability by WestJet.
“We didn’t get justice here,” said Lewis.
The case garnered national attention for exposing pilot behaviour toward female flight attendants and the vulnerability of the scores of young women who have historically been the target demographic for the job.
A 2018 survey of more than 3,500 flight attendants by the US Association of Flight Attendants found that 68% had experienced sexual harassment in their careers while only 7% had reported an incident to their employer.
WestJet did not respond to questions about Lewis’s claims of assault, and the allegations that it failed to keep the workplace free of harassment and does not properly investigate alleged sexual assaults.
In a statement, the company said it was “pleased to have reached a mutually agreed upon settlement”. It said: “We are committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and wellbeing of all WestJetters and we are focused on advancing a culture of empowerment.”

title: Europe solar eclipse live: millions flock to viewing spots in Spain, UK and Iceland
summary:
Eclipse to be witnessed by tens of millions across western Europe as enthusiasts gather along path of totality

in Land’s End, Cornwall

The roads and car parks of west and north Cornwall are clogged as people gather to watch the solar eclipse.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Lava spews as Mount Etna puts spectacular display and disrupt flights
Lorenzo Tondo
in Palermo, Sicily
For several days, Mount Etna, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, has been putting on a spectacular display, spewing incandescent magma, sending long streams of lava down its slopes and showering the surrounding area with ash.
Explosive activity has been recorded on Etna’s north-eastern flank, where new fractures have opened, while the Voragine crater has continued to produce towering plumes of ash reaching heights of about 4,500 metres.
The latest eruptive phase on Europe’s highest active volcano was continuing from vents at altitudes of 2,750 metres (9,022ft) and 2,360 metres, feeding several lava flows and creating extensive lava fields, according to Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV).
INGV’s Volcano Observatory Notice for Aviation (VONA) remained at red, its highest alert level, indicating an ongoing risk to aircraft from ash emissions.
The volcanic ash has caused widespread disruption at Catania airport, forcing the cancellation of numerous flights. On Tuesday, the ash cloud drifted as far as Malta, about 220km (140 miles) south of Etna, forcing airlines to cancel flights to the Mediterranean island at the height of the tourist season.
At the same time, the eruptions have drawn thousands of tourists to Etna, fascinated by the spectacle of fire and glowing lava illuminating the volcano after dark.
In recent years, experts have observed that Etna has been spewing so-called “primitive magma”, a term used to describe magma whose composition has changed relatively little from that of the Earth’s mantle where it formed. Rising from deeper within the volcano, this magma carries a greater concentration of gas and is therefore capable of producing the spectacularly high lava fountains that have become a feature of Etna’s recent eruptions.
While tonight’s eclipse will the “the greatest show off earth,” as the Guardian called it the last time it happened in 1999, it’s not the only show around.
People flock to Cornwall to watch the solar eclipse
Steven Morris
in Land’s End, Cornwall
The roads and car parks of west and north Cornwall are clogged as people gather to watch the solar eclipse.
Residents and holidaymakers are set to witness about 95% coverage – about 5% more than London according to the Royal Observatory, Greenwich.
And, yes, there is a shortage of eclipse glasses. There were notices on shops in Penzance saying they had none; in St Ives, dozens of people queued at a phone repair shop when it announced a new batch had arrived.
The eclipse comes with health warnings. The Falmouth coastguard has told people not to get too close to cliffs as the darkness gathers while the RNLI is advising those intending to watch from kayaks or surfboards or take an eclipse dip in the sea to remember that it is going to turn a little colder and, of course, visibility will be poorer.
There was a full eclipse in Cornwall in 1999 and civic leaders spent two years planning for it but poor weather meant there wasn’t the influx of visitors that had been expected.
Twenty seven years (and one day on), the vibe is a little more laid back but fine weather means the view of the eclipse should be excellent.
Eclipse glasses shortage hits Madrid as anticipation grows
Sam Jones
in Madrid
I can confirm that eclipse glasses are also in short supply here in Madrid.
Our local library had run out of the free glasses supplied by the city council two days ago, and an inquiry at a nearby optician was met with a rather curt “agotadas” (all gone) before we’d got to the end of the sentence.
Safety recalls have also been issued over six models of eclipse glasses that had been on sale here.
We’ve managed to buy some online and are getting ready for tonight in the mountains north of Madrid.
Younger members of the family are already impatient. It’s going to be a long, hot few hours…
1999: Beyond the clouds, a spectacle that put everything else in the shade
The last significant partial eclipse was reported in the UK in 1999.
Here is how we covered it at the time at the Guardian:
“Britain was brought to a standstill for almost an hour yesterday as millions of people left their homes, offices and factories to watch the last eclipse of the millennium.
The rush to watch the skies in the West Country and across the country resulted in the biggest power surge ever recorded on the National Grid and is estimated to have cost the country £500m in lost business.
More than a million people gathered in Cornwall and Devon for the once-in-a-lifetime event, with a last minute dash to the West Country by an estimated 60,000, bringing the total number of visitors to Cornwall to 270,000, double the normal number for August.”
For many, though, it was down to the luck of the meteorological draw whether they actually succeeded in glimpsing the eclipse through the thick cloud covering the counties.
For many, umbrellas rather than solar eclipse viewers were needed when, an hour before the eclipse, a torrential rainstorm lashed west Cornwall and heavy cloud completely blocked the view.
While the Scillies enjoyed 106 seconds of totality under clear skies, the thousands gathered in Penzance, Marazion and Falmouth found cloud and rain blotted out their view.
Within an hour of the eclipse, more than 100 people called a helpline at Moorfields Eye Hospital in London, complaining of problems after watching the solar spectacular.
Many hospitals cancelled eye operations to make way for emergencies and will remain on 24-hour standby until the weekend for worried eclipse watchers who fear they have damaged their vision.”
It’s nice of Bónus bosses to offer their employees a chance to go out and experience the eclipse.
For all we know, there isn’t usually that much interest in supermarket shopping during the phenomenon – with Waitrose chief even complaining about it in 1999, the last time we had a solar eclipse in the UK…
People flock to watch eclipse in Iceland but weather concerns dampen spirits
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
In Iceland, people have flocked by air, land and sea to watch the total solar eclipse – the country’s first in 72 years.
But the forecast is not looking promising, with low clouds expected to cover much of the country.
The eclipse will start in Iceland at about 4.45pm local time (5.45pm UK) and end at about 6.50pm (7.50pm UK).
The total eclipse will only be visible in western Iceland, with the longest in Látrabjarg in the Westfjords where it will last for 2 minutes and 13 seconds. A road in the area was closed overnight due to heavy traffic and people were not permitted to stay at the site, which is part of a nature reserve, overnight.
Record numbers of cruise ships are headed to the water around Iceland in the hope of witnessing the eclipse.
The Icelandic artist Björk is hosting a one-day festival to coincide with the eclipse at Hafnarfjörður near Reykjavík. The eclipse is featured in the set list at 5.48pm between DJ sets by Arca and Björk.
The boss of supermarket Bónuss has told store managers they can close for 15 minutes to allow employees to see the eclipse.
Where will the solar eclipse be visible in Europe?
Nicola DavisandOliver Holmes
A wide band of north and central Spain, plus a sliver of Portugal and parts of Greenland and Iceland will experience a rare total eclipse.
The light of the setting sun will be virtually blocked out across much of western Europe, including the UK, France, Belgium, Switzerland and northern Italy.
This total eclipse will be the first in mainland Europe in two decades.
The last event of this kind visible from the UK occurred in 1999, when parts of Devon and Cornwall were in the path of totality.
The next total solar eclipse visible in the UK is not due to occur until 2090.

title: In Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attention
summary:
As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Europe is in an economic crisis that, unlike the eurozone downturn at the beginning of the millennium, cannot be measured in ratings downgrades and borrowing costs. For metrics, try engagement depth and consumer trust instead.

The unedifying spectacle of the European Union’s falling out over the Ceuta crisis looks like the latest symptom of Europe’s shrinking attention economy. When more than 70,000 people crossed over from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the start of the month, Rome hastily reintroduced air and sea border checks with Spain for one month; Madrid retaliated with spot-checks on travellers to Italy.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Europe is in an economic crisis that, unlike the eurozone downturn at the beginning of the millennium, cannot be measured in ratings downgrades and borrowing costs. For metrics, try engagement depth and consumer trust instead.
The unedifying spectacle of the European Union’s falling out over the Ceuta crisis looks like the latest symptom of Europe’s shrinking attention economy. When more than 70,000 people crossed over from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the start of the month, Rome hastily reintroduced air and sea border checks with Spain for one month; Madrid retaliated with spot-checks on travellers to Italy.
Politicians were falling over themselves to match the wildfire speed of social media, for this was a geopolitical flashpoint that appears not just to have been engineered but also politically processed via short video clips online. The crossings were reportedly triggered by viral videos suggesting that Spain’s border with Morocco was opening, while their framing as an “assault” or “invasion” was amplified by accounts with links to the Russian military, as Aisha Down reported. Platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok are built to reward content that instantly hooks in viewers – three seconds long is the golden rule. How can lawmakers ever keep up?
Yet what if, paradoxically, our attention economy is both shrinking and expanding at the same time? I’ve found it hard to shake that impression after perusing the lineup at the forthcoming Venice film festival, opening on 2 September.
This year at the Lido, you can watch a three-hour film about the Italian Communist party sending a camera team to the Soviet Union (Imperium, by Ukrainian auteur Sergei Loznitsa); a four-hour documentary about Elon Musk (Musk, by American director Alex Gibney); or a more than five-hour video diary about Russian dissident journalists in exile (Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II). Too short for you? Then, get tickets for Luca Guadagnino’s Joie de Vivre, a lengthy analysis of the films of compatriot Bernardo Bertolucci. It clocks in at seven hours.
For the most part, these are surprisingly politically forthright titles at a film festival that in the recent past has focused on glitz and glamour. Loznitsa’s documentary seeks to shatter the remnants of the left’s illusions about the Soviet Union; Loktev gives a voice to the journalists silenced by Putin; Gibney’s Musk film has already been preemptively dismissed by the far-right tycoon as a “hit job”. But are they trying to stretch out attention spans so much that they risk playing only to a gallery of cinephiles?
On the topic of impactful film-making …
Perhaps there is a point between both extremes to capture people’s imaginations and attention. That’s what the Guardian is hoping to prove, in collaboration with Franco-German culture channel Arte. We are inviting film-makers to propose short-form documentaries exploring democracy in Europe today. The winning submission will be presented at the DOK Leipzig film festival at the end of October, and subsequently receive funding, editorial support and distribution through Guardian Documentaries and Arte platforms. The deadline for submissions is 14 September.
Crucially, they should be no longer than 20 minutes – a length that Jess Gormley, the Guardian’s executive producer of documentaries, argues “encourages participation and debate”. She points to recent Guardian documentaries such as Liane Aviram and Louis Hollis’s 23-minute short The Oath, about a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, which led to its protagonist being invited to speak in front of the UK parliament – a film that held, rather than overwhelmed our attention.

title: LFM2.5-VL-3B for Better and Faster Vision Capabilities for the Edge
full_text:
LFM2.5-VL-3B for Better and Faster Vision Capabilities for the Edge
LFM2.5-VL-3B extends the vision-language capabilities of our previous releases with four major improvements:
- Screen/UI understanding: Strong understanding of digital screens across different devices.
- Grounding: Improved grounding and object detection with natural language queries.
- Multi-image input: Improved reasoning across multiple images.
- Function calling: Significantly stronger at function calling, in text-only and vision-text situations.
How we trained our most capable vision-language model
LFM2.5-VL-3B pairs a SigLIP2 400M NaFlex vision encoder with the same pre-trained backbone as our LFM2.5-2.6B text model. It is pre-trained on about 34T tokens, with 4x more vision data than before, drawn from curated and synthetic image-caption, OCR, grounding, and instruction-following sets. To support non-Latin scripts, we doubled the vocabulary to 128K by extending the tokenizer in place rather than retraining from scratch.
Post-training runs in two stages: First is supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with knowledge distillation from a larger teacher and Antidoom training. Second is multi-reward reinforcement learning (RL).
Benchmark results
We evaluated LFM2.5-VL-3B across both vision and text benchmarks.
The vision benchmarks cover multilingual visual comprehension, instruction following, visual math and scientific reasoning, document understanding, object detection, multi-image understanding, and screen understanding. LFM2.5-VL-3B leads its size class on real-world image tasks, while also reading digital content well, from documents and charts to on-screen UI elements.
*All values in the table are normalized to 0–100. Evaluation is done using vLLM 0.26.0 and each model’s recommended generation parameters when available. Non-reasoning mode is used everywhere, and models are prompted to directly answer without reasoning.
We also evaluated LFM2.5-VL-3B on text-only benchmarks for instruction following and tool use. Instruction following climbs across the board, and tool use improves sharply. On tool use, LFM2.5-VL-3B is on par with Gemma-4-E2B and Qwen3.5-2B.
*InternVL 3.5 models do not support function-calling.
These results demonstrate that LFM2.5-VL-3B is a strong, general-purpose vision-language model. It covers everyday tasks (captioning, visual question answering, document understanding) and is especially good at grounding objects, reading screens and documents, and calling tools.
Inference speed on CPU and GPU
LFM2.5-VL-3B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.
On-device inference. LFM2.5-VL-3B decodes 228 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 116 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395, and fits in about 3 GB of memory. It even reaches 20 tokens/s on a Galaxy S26 Ultra, so you can run it fully on-device.
GPU inference. LFM2.5-VL-3B keeps latency consistently low and is the fastest on multi-frame inputs.
LFM2.5-VL-3B is also the fastest on output throughput out of all models we tested, reaching about 11K tokens per second at high concurrency. That is roughly 2× the larger 4B-class models and ahead of even the smaller 2B-class models, which adds up to nearly 1B output tokens per day on a single H100.
How to use LFM2.5-VL-3B
Reach for LFM2.5-VL-3B when you need on-device intelligence for high-volume workloads.
Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):
%pip install -q torch torchvision accelerate "transformers>=5.10.1"
Then load and run the model:
import torch
from transformers.image_utils import load_image
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor
from IPython.display import display
MODEL_ID = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-VL-3B" 
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    device_map="auto",
    dtype="bfloat16",
)
img_url = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/coco_sample.png"
input_image = load_image(img_url)
display(input_image)
messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": input_image},
            {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image in two concise sentences."},
        ],
    }
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        do_sample=True,
        temperature=0.2,
        top_k=50,
        repetition_penalty=1.0,
        max_new_tokens=256,
    )
output = processor.batch_decode(outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)[0]
print(output)
Two cats are sleeping on a pink couch with two remote controls.
You can find more hands-on examples on how to use LFM2.5-VL3B for multi-image inputs, grounding, OCR, tool calling, and more in our documentation. Check out our release blog for video examples.
LFM2.5-VL-3B demo
Check out this browser demo of LFM2.5-VL-3B powering a vision-capable chat interface. It allows you to take or upload multiple images and let the model interact with them, including grounding, OCR, and tool use.
Get Started
LFM2.5-VL-3B is available on Hugging Face today.
With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:
- Download: LFM2.5-VL-3B on Hugging Face.
- Try: run the WebGPU demo in your browser, no setup needed.
- Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-VL-3B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials.
We can't wait to see what you build.

title: Google aims for influencers with the Pixel 11 Creator Suite
summary: Google knows creators are a big audience. The occupation is growing fast, and landing some influential names could be a major turning point for the Pixel's market share. This year, Google is building features directly into its new Pixel lineup that it says can help creators record, organize, edit, and publish content faster and more […]
full_text:
Google knows creators are a big audience. The occupation is growing fast, and landing some influential names could be a major turning point for the Pixel’s market share. This year, Google is building features directly into its new Pixel lineup that it says can help creators record, organize, edit, and publish content faster and more efficiently than they could on other devices.
Google aims for influencers with the Pixel 11 Creator Suite
The new phones are getting a bundle of features designed to help burgeoning influencers film and edit content.
Creator Suite is a new mode built into the Pixel 11’s camera app. The suite comes with features like a teleprompter, vocal enhancer, external microphone levels, and social media frame guides, which Google thinks will entice users who want to start building channels and have limited resources.
“ We really wanted to do something for those folks who are creating on their phones to make it easier to do that, make it faster to publish, fewer retakes, easier organization, and just streamline that workflow,” Isaac Reynolds, who leads the Pixel camera team, tells The Verge.
Reynolds says there is a massive gap between the top and bottom of the creator market, where the biggest creators have teams and resources, but the “hundreds of thousands of creators” in the bottom of the market need more accessible ways to make content.
“ They’re striving to put out content weekly or daily, even when they have full-time jobs,” Reynolds says. “They’ve got money coming in, it’s very enticing, but it’s not the replacement for their work yet.”
The arrival of TikTok has fundamentally reshaped what it means to be an influencer or a content creator, and the barrier to entry to do that work is lower than ever; all you need to do is film a selfie video. Over the last five or so years, the creator industry has both professionalized and de-professionalized: Influencers are signed to talent agencies and retain professional management, but there’s also been an explosion of cheap and fast content that is not tied to a specific personality — all that matters is whether it’s being served up to audiences. AI slop is everywhere. Follower count is increasingly irrelevant, and making content for the internet is, in theory, an attainable job for anyone, including people with other full-time jobs. Google recognizes that and wants those legions of people to use its phone.
Google has tried to court this demographic before, at least indirectly: Last year, it tapped Alex Cooper, host of the popular celebrity interview podcast Call Her Daddy, to make Google ads and post selfies on Instagram with the Pixel (she also promoted photo editing features at Made By Google last year). The partnership touted how Google’s ecosystem would help Cooper’s business as a content creator — scripting videos, shooting content, and keeping her team organized. Google now wants to reach the individuals who are pumping out content by themselves with just a phone.
Photography by David Imel / The Verge

title: The 7 biggest announcements of Google’s Pixel 11 launch
summary: Google is hosting a Pixel launch event on Wednesday night where it will show off its latest lineup of devices. But you don't have to wait until then for all the news: We were able to check out the devices ahead of the event and take a look at everything Google's unveiling, including the latest […]
full_text:
Google is hosting a Pixel launch event on Wednesday night where it will show off its latest lineup of devices. But you don’t have to wait until then for all the news: We were able to check out the devices ahead of the event and take a look at everything Google’s unveiling, including the latest Pixel phones, new health features on the Pixel Watch 5, and more.
The 7 biggest announcements of Google’s Pixel 11 launch
This year’s Made by Google event featured a new lineup of Pixel phones and updates to the Pixel Watch and Buds.
Google will be livestreaming the event on Wednesday at 6PM ET / 3PM PT. But if you aren’t able to watch along yourself, you can catch up on all of the highlights from Wednesday’s Pixel launch below.
Google refreshed its line of Pixel phones, starting with the Pixel 11. The design didn’t change drastically compared to the Pixel 10, although it now comes in a few new colors, including a lilac-like frost, hibiscus pink, and pistachio green, along with obsidian black. It runs on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which Google claims offers 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent faster app loading. Google also says its battery lasts over 30 hours and supports 25 percent faster wireless charging than the Pixel 10.
The Pixel 11 also features an upgraded camera and a camera bump that’s over 40 percent thinner than the Pixel 10’s. It includes 48MP wide, 13MP ultra-wide, and 10.8MP 5x telephoto lenses on the back and a 10.5MP selfie camera on the front. Google says the 48MP wide lens has 56 percent more light sensitivity and the 5x telephoto lens supports up to 30x Super Zoom.
Unfortunately, the Pixel 11 also got a $100 price bump — it now starts at $899, but the base configuration has 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, rather than the 128GB of storage in the Pixel 10’s starting configuration. It launches on August 20th.
Google’s Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL include a new feature in the camera bar called HiLight, which is an LED indicator light for things like Gemini interactions and incoming calls from favorite contacts. Google says the little LED will get more capabilities down the line, like signaling message notifications from frequent contacts.
The Pixel 11 Pro also features an upgraded display that maxes out at 3,600 nits. Inside, it has Google’s Tensor G6 chip like the base Pixel 11. The camera includes a new 48MP telephoto lens with up to 120x Pro Zoom and a new 50MP wide lens, along with a 48MP ultra-wide lens and a 42MP selfie camera. According to Google, it offers over 30 hours of battery life and over 29 percent faster wireless charging compared to the Pixel 10 Pro / Pro XL.
The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 with 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM while the Pro XL starts at $1,299 with the same specs. The 512GB and 1TB storage options include 16GB of RAM. The Pro and Pro XL are both available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and matte obsidian.
Google says the Pixel 11 Pro Fold features the thinnest bezels ever on a Fold and claims it’s three times as durable as the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, with IP68 water and dust resistance and a back material that’s “designed to be nearly impossible to crack.”
The Fold’s displays are 20 percent brighter than last year’s model and the inner display goes up to 3,600 nits of brightness like the Pixel 11 Pro / Pro XL. It also runs on Google’s Tensor G6 chip and offers up to 24 hours of battery life. The camera includes a new 48MP wide lens plus a 10.5MP ultra-wide lens and a 10.8MP telephoto lens with up to 30x Super Zoom.
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs $100 more than last year’s model, starting at $1,899 for a base configuration with 256GB of storage and 16GB of RAM and two color options: olive and black.
In addition to hardware upgrades, Google’s also introducing some new features for taking photos and videos across its new lineup of phones. The Camera app has a new capture mode called Magic Capture that can pull photos and clips out of video recordings.
There are also Camera Looks, which offers customizable, stylized photo presets that change how your phone processes the photo, rather than simply applying a filter. The various Looks include styles like minimal, editorial, and “digi,” which mimics digital cameras. The Pixel 11 Pro also has a new Pro Stable Video feature Google says can record at up to 8K.
A new Creator tab in the Camera app has a “Creator Suite” with tools for trimming and reordering videos, an onscreen teleprompter, and improved Speech Enhancement.
The new Pixel Watch 5 might look essentially the same as the previous version, but it includes some major new software features. Breathing Emergency Detection, a follow-up to last year’s Loss of Pulse feature, can trigger an emergency call if the watch detects a significant, sustained drop in blood oxygen saturation (SpO2). The Pixel Watch 5 can also track nightly sleep breathing quality and sum up the data in monthly reports. Starting in September, Google’s also introducing Blood Pressure Trends and Insulin Resistance Trends.
The Pixel Watch 5 has some new workout features, as well, like AI-generated strength training plans and the option to track reps directly from your watch. Google claims it includes the “most accurate GPS route tracking for exercise, outperforming Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro.”
Unfortunately, this year’s Pixel Watch is a little pricier — it got a $50 price bump and now starts at $399. It’s available in two sizes, 45mm and 41mm, and four colors: black, white, olive green, and pink. There’s also a Steph Curry special edition that costs $579 and launches a bit later on September 3rd.
Google’s taking on Apple’s AirTag with the Pixel Tag, its own item tracker, launching on November 11th for $29 individually or $99 for a pack of four. It’s oblong rather than round, measuring 1.1 inches by 1.8 inches (the AirTag is 1.26 inches across). The tracker is IP67 water and dust resistant and Google says its replaceable CR2032 coin cell battery lasts over a year.
Google is releasing the two-year-old Pixel Buds Pro 2 in a new olive green color on August 12th, which matches the olive Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold. In September, Google’s also rolling out a firmware update for the Buds Pro 2 that’s supposed to improve the earbuds’ Active Noise Cancellation.

title: Google’s Pixel 11 series pairs a little new hardware with a lot of new software
summary: When I first picked up the Pixel 11 Pro this week, it was clear to me that this was one of those refinement years - at least when it comes to hardware. Aesthetically, the phones are as beautiful as ever, with Google's signature camera bar and bright, colorful backing glass. There are small updates, like […]
full_text:
When I first picked up the Pixel 11 Pro this week, it was clear to me that this was one of those refinement years — at least when it comes to hardware. Aesthetically, the phones are as beautiful as ever, with Google’s signature camera bar and bright, colorful backing glass. There are small updates, like a single piece of glass covering the camera bar and the all-new HiLight ambient LED on the Pros. But this year, the Pixel is all about quality of life and software improvements.
Google’s Pixel 11 series pairs a little new hardware with a lot of new software
More helpful features, less AI slop.
Google’s Pixel 11 series pairs a little new hardware with a lot of new software
More helpful features, less AI slop.
After weeks of teasers, Google has finally formally announced the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The phones are all shipping next week, on August 20th, and Google is holding a splashy event the evening of August 12th to show off the devices. Ahead of that, we had a chance to take a first look at everything that’s coming up.
Pixel 11
Let’s start with the bad news up front: All of these phones are $100 more expensive than last year’s. Google has killed off the 128GB base storage option this year, which means the Pixel 11 now starts at $899 for a 256GB model. All storage tiers still come with 12GB of RAM, but the higher entry price is no doubt driven by RAMageddon, which has been increasing costs across the industry.
If you can look past the price, you’ll find a refined version of last year’s phone that looks and feels a bit more premium. The camera bar is now made of a singular piece of glass and is over 40 percent thinner. If you use it with one of Google’s cases, the bar will become completely flush. (This gives you three different camera bar thickness options on the Pixel line now, which only get thicker the more premium you go.)
The cameras have been upgraded, too. On the Pixel 11, the 48MP wide is quoted with 56 percent more light gathering capability from its new 1/1.56-inch sensor, and the 5x telephoto lens can now digitally zoom up to 30x, which Google says is enabled by the new image signal processor in the Tensor G6 chipset. And considering the new Tensor G6 chip is said to be up to 20 percent more efficient, Google is quoting up to 30-plus hours of battery life across the lineup.
Perhaps the most interesting update to me is the new Camera Looks feature. You can think of this similarly to the film recipes on Fujifilm cameras, presenting users with stylized presets that can be customized to their liking.
What makes Camera Looks so interesting, though, is instead of just being a filter on top of the preprocessed Pixel photo, the phone will process the photo completely differently at the sensor level depending on which settings you choose, potentially using less frame stacking and sharpening to deliver the photo you actually want. During my briefing at least, this really delivered. The Natural mode does an amazing job of lowering the sharpness and contrast and making the photos look much more true to life, and I’m excited to take it for a proper spin later. If you want to learn more about this, check out my dedicated article where I spoke with Pixel camera lead Isaac Reynolds.
Another new feature inside the camera is Magic Capture. This is a camera mode alongside the photo and video modes that creates a sort of hybrid mashup of the two, where the phone will automatically pick out short clips and images you can share. During my hands-on time this feature didn’t work great, only giving me one small clip and one photo from a roughly 15-second recording, but I believe it’s meant for longer clips at things like kids’ birthday parties. We’ll have to test this in the field once we have more time with the device.
Google is also adding a new Creator Suite inside the camera, which gives you access to tools like social media framing guides, speech enhancement, a teleprompter, and automatic folder structures for video. I was surprised to see this so deeply integrated into the camera itself, and it’s clear Google is going after a new audience and hoping to make the Pixel the best phone for small creators.
The phones also all feature Qi2.2 — an upgrade from Qi2 last year. Google says this offers 25 percent faster wireless charging of up to 25W, an upgrade from the 15W max the Pixel 10 offered. However, many users reported seeing a maximum wireless charge rate of only 5W with the Pixel 10 when using older chargers, so hopefully the problem is fixed this year.
The Pixel 11 will come in purple, green, black, and an extremely hot magenta.
Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL
The 11 Pro and Pro XL are where things get a little more interesting this year. Like the standard Pixel 11, they start at 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM (down from 16GB last year), which starts at $1,099. If you’re a power user, you can still get 16GB of RAM if you buy the 512GB or 1TB models.
You’re definitely getting more with the Pro models this year, though. The display on the Pixel 11 Pro gets up to a super bright 3,600 nits, which Google says is the brightest display ever on a smartphone. This isn’t a massive difference from the 3,300-nit peak brightness from last year, but it’s something for your money.
The main camera sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro has been improved, with a new 50MP model that Google says uses less power and should perform better in the 1x-to-5x zoom range. There’s also a new 48MP telephoto lens with a larger 1/1.95-inch sensor that delivers a quoted 30 percent improvement in light sensitivity. And just like the standard Pixel 11, the 11 Pro has a further zoom range, now extending up to 120x, which Google says is enabled by the ISP in Tensor G6.
On the Pro phones, Google has also substantially sped up Night Sight, offering up to 4.5x faster low-light image capture, though Google tells me on average it’s about 3x faster than last year. This is still a pretty substantial improvement, and Reynolds told me the idea was to optimize Night Sight for handheld capture. “You can still capture for up to four minutes if you want all the light,” he tells me, “but it’s really optimized for those awkward moments where you have to tell someone to hold still for a little too long.”
The flashiest feature (pun intended) of the new Pro phones is the HiLight feature. Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold phones now feature an RGB LED ring where the temperature sensor used to be on the right side of the camera bar. When you’re talking to Gemini, the LED will glow blue as it listens and responds to you. Separately, you can set favorite contacts to glow when they call you through the default Phone app or WhatsApp. Google is marketing the feature as a way to be more present in your everyday life, but it doesn’t feel particularly useful to me yet considering its use is so limited. Google says more functionality is coming in the future, but right now, this doesn’t feel like a reason to buy the phone.
The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL will come in olive, light blue, and a striking orange-ish “canyon” color, all with glossy side rails. There’s also a black option, which this year has matte side rails, unlike all the other Pro devices.
Pixel 11 Pro Fold
Finally, there’s the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google is calling it the most durable Pixel Fold yet, with a new composite back material that Google says is nearly impossible to crack. This, alongside a thicker inner ultra-thin glass display, contributes to Google’s “3x more durable” claim compared to last year.
The inner bezels have also been reduced, making it Google’s thinnest Fold bezels ever, and the peak brightness matches the Pixel 11 Pro at 3,600 nits. The 11 Pro Fold is also inheriting the new 48MP main sensor from the Pixel 11 for a quoted 56 percent improved light sensitivity compared to last year, and it gets Qi2.2 for up to 20 percent faster wireless charging.
