title: 亞利桑那加密 ATM 退款法：35 人拿回 17.1 萬鎂，30 天內通報才有效
summary:
亞利桑那州 2025 年 9 月生效的加密 ATM 退款法，10 個月內已協助 35 名詐騙受害者拿回總計 1 […]

〈亞利桑那加密 ATM 退款法：35 人拿回 17.1 萬鎂，30 天內通報才有效〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
亞利桑那州 2025 年 9 月生效的加密 ATM 退款法，10 個月內已協助 35 名詐騙受害者拿回總計 17.1 萬美元。新客戶在 30 天內通報可全額退費，但每日限額僅 2,000 美元。
（前情提要：加密 ATM 詐騙老人百萬美元！美國明尼蘇達州禁令正式生效）
（背景補充：FBI：美國加密 ATM 詐騙去年破 3.3 億美元，多州掀禁令潮）
亞利桑那州總檢察長辦公室週三公布，自 2025 年 9 月 26 日加密 ATM 退款法生效以來，已有 35 名詐騙受害者成功取得全額退款，總計 171,332 美元。
亞利桑那州總檢察長 Kris Mayes 在宣告中表示，辦公室已協助這批受害者完成退款程式，並呼籲民眾若遭詐騙應立即通報，以免錯過法定的 30 天申請期限。
退款資格與申請條件
依據 House Bill 2387 規範，加密 ATM 業者必須為符合條件的新客戶退還因受騙而進行的交易款項，並包含相關手續費。
申請退款需滿足以下條件：
- 新客戶定義：使用該 ATM 業者的天數少於 10 天
- 通報期限：交易後 30 天內聯絡業者與總檢察長辦公室或其他執法單位
- 詐騙認定：須提供官方報告，確認受害者係因受詐騙誘導而進行交易
- 退費範圍：全額退還交易金額，含手續費
新舊客戶限額差異
同一法規也針對新舊客戶設定不同的每日交易上限：
- 新客戶：每日最高 2,000 美元
- 既存客戶：每日最高 10,500 美元
限額落差反映了立法者對風險的判斷：首次接觸加密 ATM 的使用者更容易成為詐騙目標，因而給予較高的保護力度與較低的風險敞口。
全美 ATM 詐騙現況與亞州做法對比
亞利桑那州的退款法並非孤立現象。根據 FBI 2025 年初公布的資料，美國加密 ATM 詐騙案在 2024 年損失超過 3.3 億美元，多州已跟進立法或禁令。
明尼蘇達州於 2026 年 8 月全面禁止加密 ATM，理由是保護老年人免受詐騙；密蘇里州總檢察長則於同年 5 月正式起訴 ATM 業者 CoinFlip，指控其裝置成為詐騙與洗錢工具，最高求償 182.6 萬美元。
與明州「一刀切禁令」的路徑不同，亞利桑那州採取的是業者責任 + 消費者救濟的混合模式：不禁止加密 ATM 營運，但要求業者承擔退款義務，同時給受害者明確的救濟管道。從已退還 17.1 萬美元的資料來看，這條路徑至少在短期內產出了可量化的成果。
後續觀察：30 天期限與實際詐騙模式
30 天通報期限是這套機制最關鍵的限制。許多加密詐騙（尤其是殺豬盤或遠端遙控型）的受害者往往在事件發生數週甚至數月後才意識到自己被騙，到時已超出退款視窗。
另一個變數是「官方詐騙認定報告」的取得門檻。如果執法單位的調查節奏緩慢，受害者可能卡在「已通報但尚未拿到認定檔案」的狀態，導致退款流程無法啟動。Mayes 辦公室後續是否會針對這類邊緣案例推出緩衝機制，值得關注。
亞利桑那州的實驗如果持續跑出正面資料，可能成為其他州仿效的模板，在不扼殺加密 ATM 產業的前提下，用業者責任機制把詐騙損失控制在可承受範圍。

title: Travis Kelce shares first details from his wedding to Taylor Swift - 'Best night of my life'
summary: In the comments, Kelce called Swift his "wife" for first time and said it was a "childhood dream" to wed at Madison Square Garden.
full_text:
Travis Kelce shares first details from his wedding to Taylor Swift - 'Best night of my life'
- Published
American football player Travis Kelce has reflected on his wedding to Taylor Swift, telling US media that their nuptials were "the best night of my life".
Kelce and Swift tied the knot on 3 July at New York's Madison Square Garden in a star-studded event that was largely kept private.
Few details from the ceremony have been shared publicly and Kelce's comments on Wednesday mark the first he's shared since the couple were wed by comedic actor Adam Sandler.
"It was kind of cool to live out my childhood dream of being in that venue, the mecca of all sports venues, being able to get married there," Kelce told reporters at the Kansas City Chiefs' training camp in Missouri.
Kelce called the wedding "the best night of my life", thanking guests who attended and calling it "a crazy night".
The NFL star and the award-winning singer have kept much of the details of the wedding private and there have been no official photos released of the ceremony held inside the stadium. A litany of Hollywood A-list stars, such as actors Hugh Grant and Jason Sudeikis, singer Benson Boone and model Gigi Hadid were in attendance.
Kelce said he had wanted to attend a game when the New York Knicks basketball team were having a good playoff run last year, but had other commitments. The team ended up winning the NBA championships for the first time in nearly six decades.
"My wife went when I was stuck in a mini camp so I didn't get my opportunity to go then," he said referring to Swift as his wife publicly for the first time. She sat courtside at Game 4 of the NBA Finals, when the Knicks pulled off a stunning upset against the San Antonio Spurs in a 107-106 finish.
"I can't thank the owners of MSG enough for allowing us to get the opportunity to do that, knowing that we wanted a private event and everything, and it was perfect," he added.
Later, he joked that the "AC was cooking" inside the venue, an apparent reference to the heatwave that swept over the country over the Independence Day weekend.
The couple's nuptials were shrouded in secrecy despite the event shutting down a part of New York City - the most populous city in the US. Much of the event still was wrapped in uncertainty as to whether the couple had already wed in days prior or whether the event might just be a party.
But hours after a lengthy list of celebrities were seen entering the venue in gowns and suits, large screens attached to the arena announced publicly that the famous couple were officially wed.
Kelce noted "it was a fun off-season" but said he was now excited to return to training and American football.
Kelce, who turns 37 in October, has won three Super Bowl championships with the Chiefs.
The team did not make the NFL playoffs last year for the first time in 10 seasons. Many believe the upcoming season, which begins next month, could be his last. But the tight end hasn't said whether retirement could be next.
"I have still got a lot of love for this game," he said. "I want to go out there and prove to myself that I can play at a better level than I did last year."
"This is always going to be my sanctuary," he said of being back on the field. "You need to have this time of grinding with the guys, being around them all day, starting to create that chemistry and standard for how we are going to do things. This year it's ramped up even more.

title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplants
summary: NHS Blood and Transplant's medical director says waiting lists for organ operations are unfair but leaders are not solving the issue.
full_text:
Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplants
- Published
A senior doctor has blamed NHS chiefs for numerous problems within transplant services in England and called for an overhaul in a leaked letter seen by the BBC.
Professor Derek Manas, the medical director of NHS Blood and Transplant, admonished NHS England for creating a system with a burnt-out workforce, "few consequences for poor performance" and operations cancelled "last-minute".
The number of heart and lung transplants the NHS carries out each year has not increased in 30 years.
NHS England, the national management body for the health service in England, said it was "working hard to improve these life-saving services".
'Unpredictable' utilising of organs
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.
But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".
There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.
This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.
The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.
The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.
It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.
Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.
Waiting times for donated hearts can vary greatly - from eight months to four-and-a-half years - depending on the hospital.
Manas said NHS England had "never actively managed" waiting lists, and "seldom" tried to make it fairer.
In addition, half of the six UK heart and lung transplantation centres have lost their top surgeon in the past two years, as the medics seek opportunities abroad.
Manas said "inadequate" workforce planning had led to "burnout among transplant surgeons and teams, recruitment and retention difficulties [and] increasing reliance on goodwill. We have a system that assumes the consultant workforce will absorb pressure indefinitely."
Issues in the heart and lung transplantation service were first outlined in 2024 in a report by international experts, commissioned by the Conservative government.
NHS England, which was tasked with implementing report recommendations, said it had worked to "improve outcomes for patients", but surgeons and campaigners believe progress has been slow.
Among those who believe the system should change is Dr Zubir Ahmed, who was the health minister responsible for transplantation until he quit Sir Keir Starmer's government in May.
The Glasgow MP and kidney transplant surgeon told the BBC some elements of the transplant system were "world leading", such as being free at the point of care.
But he called for NHS Blood and Transplant to be granted the power to commission services across the UK as part of ministers' planned closure of NHS England, so that patients could be moved swiftly to get the organ they need.
"I don't think there is ever a need to cancel a transplant because of capacity issues," Ahmed said.
In a statement, NHS England said transplant services are "complex and impacted by many factors, including the number of organs made available for transplantation, but the NHS is working hard to improve these lifesaving services".
"NHS England is leading a programme of work which is already helping to increase the number of transplants, reduce variation, identify suitable patients earlier and improve access," it added.

title: 'If you're not conservative, don't come here': The town making missiles for Trump
summary: The president's approval numbers may be down, but in this Tennessee town, his support is as strong as ever.
full_text:
'If you're not conservative, don't come here': The town making missiles for Trump
- Published
As one local puts it, there's a "church on every street" of the Appalchian community of Kingsport, in the US state of Tennessee.
Christianity reigns supreme in this working-class area. Above downtown's historic Lamplight Theatre, a sign proclaims "Jesus first in all things".
And while more than 300 area churches may be providing spiritual sustenance to this town of 58,000 people, there's another institution that supplies it with economic nourishment.
The Holston Army Ammunition Plant churns out explosives used in Patriot missiles, warheads and other heavy weaponry in the midst of the country's costly and prolonged war with Iran.
The war, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Recent polling has placed his approval at an historic low of 32% - down 14% from when he first took office in January 2025 - with many Republican respondents citing disillusionment with the president's policies.
The two big drags on the president's popularity are the cost of living and the Iran War, with one bleeding into the other. The conflict has caused gas prices in the US to spike to above $4 a gallon, a painful hike to any US business that relies on transport.
But in Kingsport, support for the president approaches an almost-religious fervor. The city voted overwhelmingly for Trump in all three of his elections. So did wider Tennessee, a Republican state for more than 25 years.
When it comes to the Iran conflict, most residents either outright support the military action or rationalise the war's necessity - despite Trump's repeated campaign promise of "no more wars".
"If he can stop anyone from having a nuclear bomb, then I'm for it," says Pam Robinson, 65, who spent 20 years working at the local chemical plant.
David Carter, a bearded veteran who plays Santa Claus at Christmastime, says "the whole reason we go over there, and we keep everything under control there, is [so that] we don't have it on our doorstep."
Others are more blunt.
"Honestly, I think we should turn them into a parking lot and don't worry about it anymore," says veteran James Camper, 63, wearing a Trump lanyard around his neck as he exits a discount grocery.
Veterans account for around 10% of the region's population, and many other households have active duty family members.
Robinson, a staunch Christian and independent voter who says her faith informs her candidate choices, believes the remote nature of the war may be preventing local people from being more upset with Trump.
"Let me say this: If it was hand-to-hand and more people were getting killed, people would be banging the doors down," she says.
Kingsport's position as a main munitions manufacturer - with Holston standing as the only domestic supplier of some essential explosive and propellant components - gives its residents a unique perspective when it comes to the war in Iran.
The plant employs around 1,000 people and is just one of many sprawling industrial complexes standing out starkly from the lush Appalachian Mountain landscape.
"The plant's going to be open regardless of whether we're at war or whether we're not," says Daniel Overstreet, 53, standing next to his Harley Davidson in downtown Kingsport. "It is what it is."
He believes Trump and the administration are "doing a great job" but there are "too many people trying to fight him."
"[He said] he would get the gas prices under control, and they were for a while," says Overstreet. "He said he was gonna get food prices down, but he has no control over that. The president is basically a puppet for Congress and the Senate.
"His hands are tied, to a certain extent."
It's not that people here don't complain about high gas and food prices, inflation and other economic woes - it's just they don't blame Trump for any of it.
"He's done good on some things; I think he needs to check his advisers and see on some things," says Robinson. "I think he's advised wrong on some things."
It was Trump himself, however, who announced his decision to strike Iran in February 2026 following failed negotiations. In an eight-minute video posted to social media, he said "the objective is to defend the American people by eliminating imminent threats from the Iranian regime" - and claimed Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon".
Evangelist William Bogle, 75, voted for Trump every time he ran and believes the president is "doing a good job" - even though his wife "has to stretch a grocery dollar until, you know, it's big as a bedsheet".
Trump is "just gonna have to do a little bit better in some things than he's doing right now," he says.
"I know he wants the country to prosper."
This stalwart support reflects a deeper truth sometimes hidden in the polling headlines. Although Trump has lost favour among more traditional Republicans and independent voters, his base - who self-identify with his "Make America Great Again" mantra - remains much more steadfast in backing him.
So while much of the US watches to see how much Trump's sliding popularity may damage Republicans in November's midterm elections, here in the Bible Belt, sometimes red is the only option.
As voters turned out last week for local elections, the ballot included a single Democratic candidate. Of the county commission's 11 districts, seven featured only Republicans running, with some unopposed.
Many say they can't and won't cross party lines for moral reasons, citing abortion as the single biggest deciding factor, with opposition to socialism and "woke" issues too hard for them to ignore.
Those fears outweigh any personal criticisms they may have, says David Carter, 66, a grandfather and Christian as well as a veteran.
Trump needs to humble himself more, he concedes, but Carter would only consider a candidate who "supports the morals" of the population. That means opposing abortion, for example.
Those who hold more liberal views exist in Kingsport, but they're vastly in the minority and less vocal.
Piercing artist Adam Teague, 44, is a gay, heavily-tattooed Democrat working in downtown Kingsport.
"Before Trump took office, I was wearing, like, rainbow shirts and everything," says Teague, who was raised Baptist. "I kind of toned it down, just to feel safer."
Trump was triumphant in the 2024 election in part because of his ability to attract a diverse coalition including people of all ages and races. But while his Maga supporters are sticking by him, polling suggests that many young people who helped get him over the line against Kamala Harris are now disillusioned.
Mary Herron, 21, who is leaving a boutique cupcake shop with two friends, has noticed a difference in attitudes amongst her contemporaries.
"I am seeing a shift in the support … that's kind of rare around here," says Herron, a student who works part-time. "But I've seen a handful of people who have been like, 'Oh yeah, well, I voted for him, and now I'm not with him anymore'."
Trump first entered politics when the women were in middle school, says her friend Emily Villalpando, 21. "So a lot of the people that we grew up with kind of just adopted their parents' views.
"And so now that we're growing up, we're having more responsibilities," says Villalpando, who's studying biomedical science and wants to be a doctor. "The economy affects us a lot more."
The three college students - their friend Caden Bayless makes up the trio - cite women's rights and heavy-handed immigration agents as major concerns, but they are sceptical of major attitude or voting shifts in the region.
Bayless said she is hopeful the younger generation can make a change, but "given where we live … it would be a very difficult change."

title: Ayra Starr on her secret relationship and teasing Stevie Wonder
summary: The musician shares the personal stories behind her third album, and the time she teased a legend.
full_text:
Ayra Starr on her secret relationship and teasing Stevie Wonder
- Published
There's resilience, and then there's Ayra Starr.
Two weeks before the release of her new album, Starrgirl, the Nigerian singer posted a photo from hospital, after undergoing "major surgery".
"I was hoping it would be a quick recovery, but it was more complicated than they expected," she told fans, external, without disclosing the nature of the procedure.
Within seven days, she was back in the dance studio, rehearsing for forthcoming performances with a large bandage strapped across her stomach. TV appearances, fan events and live performances followed.
"I'm healing," she told the US breakfast TV show, Today. "I have strength today. I'm so happy I was able to even be here today and be able to do this."
It's a display of the tenacity and ambition that's defined Starr's career to date.
Discovered singing covers on YouTube at the age of 18, she became the first African woman to win best international act at the Mobo Awards, and the first Nigerian woman to surpass one billion video views on YouTube.
In 2024, she was the first Afrobeats artist to play Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage – and finished her set by declaring she'd return as a headliner. Last year, she modelled for Di Petsa at London Fashion Week, closing their show in a white lace two-piece, flanked by an angel.
So it's hardly a surprise that Starr pitches up to our interview with a sort of celestial confidence. She's given to grand proclamations like "I'm unstoppable", or "I will exist in multitudes". But somehow, she never sounds arrogant or conceited.
That's probably due to a sense of humour so dry it could soak up a tsunami. Starr is criminally sarcastic, and delights in winding people up.
For example: When music legend Stevie Wonder phoned to congratulate Starr on a Grammy nomination, she goaded him into a playful argument about zodiac signs.
"I was trying to one-up him every single time, and he was trying to one-up me. It was almost like a battle," she recalls.
Starr eventually got to the point where she told Wonder, a Taurus, that "Tauruses ain't crap".
"I'm sure he was like, 'Who is this? What do you want from me?' But it was a very cute conversation. I respect it."
It's an unorthodox approach to making friends, but it seems to work.
Over the course of her career, Starr's hooked up with Coldplay, Tyla, David Guetta, Le Sserafim and Kelly Rowland from Destiny's Child.
Her new album boasts collaborations with Afrobeats legends Wizkid and Rema, as well as One Direction's Zayn Malik and rising R&B singer KWN.
The album is her first under a new management deal with Jay-Z's Roc Nation, and a relocation to New York. Leaving Lagos was a big upheaval, she confessed in an essay posted to her Substack last year., external
"New York is basically a walk-in freezer with rent," she wrote. "It's so cold it feels like the city is actively trying to unalive my motivation… I'm not scared, I promise."
Secret relationship
Behind the move was a desire to explore new influences and expand her sound. So you get a track like Where Do We Go, which marries a sashaying Afrobeats rhythm to a hypnotic electronic pulse.
"Like, the rebel I am, I love to juxtapose," she says.
"I don't like being normal and boring. So the idea of writing a heartbreak song on a beat like that, where you can dance to it, was just very enticing. I love things like that."
The lyrics were inspired by a secretive relationship "that was stuck in a rut but I kept coming back to it".
We've all been there. It's all too easy to settle for an imperfect partner because they're a comfortable and familiar presence.
Starr admits the thought of starting over with someone else filled her with fear.
"You're back to square one, and somebody's asking for your favourite colour again.
"I'm like, 'Oh my God! Can we, like, not do that?'"
The problem with staying in the relationship, however, was the way it affected the rest of her life.
"You keep accepting things lower than your standard, and that influences every single thing in your life - because when you let yourself go, romantically and emotionally, it affects you physically, and the music, and all of that.
"So even though I enjoyed [the romance] while it lasted, I picked my priorities and what was most important to me. And that relationship wasn't as important as the music... or anything else."
The story could act as a metaphor for the entire album. After the runaway success of her breakout single, Rush, and her second album, The Year I Turned 21, Starr was beginning to feel trapped by other people's expectations.
"Just like any other pop artist, passive listeners get attached to the songs they know - the popular songs.
"Then you're stuck between creating for the passive listeners and creating for your core fans who want you to do more.
"So that can limit you, because you stop thinking as an artist and start thinking about making music just for consumers.
"But I'm not meant to conform. It's just not who I am. I will rebel against every single preconception and every stereotype."
So she's ditched the teenage angst of her debut, but also the poise of its follow-up. This is an album about walking to her own rhythm, as Starr grows into autonomy and womanhood.
On Misunderstood, she laughs at the people who told her she'd "never make it on her own"; while the laid back groove of Treasure allows Starr to pause and savour her success.
"Give me some fun / Pure enjoyment / Take a photo of me," she sings in Yoraba.
The most infectious song on the album is Ms Paper, which takes a detour into Bouyon – a Dominican music characterised by high tempos and frantic percussion. It was recorded almost by accident at the end of a session with French-Congolese star Theodora on a hot and sticky February night in LA.
They'd actually finished working for the day, and had just polished off a boozy dinner of Congolese food when inspiration struck.
"The AC in the studio wasn't working, so everybody's delirious, everybody's sweating, everybody's drunk," Starr says.
"At one point we're probably taking off tops. I changed outfit twice because I was drenched in sweat."
It sounds like a recipe for disaster, but when you play it back, you can practically see the steam rising from your speakers.
Live snippets of the song have already gone viral, suggesting Starr has another hefty hit on her hands. At the same time, she's faced criticism in Nigeria from people who feel she's diluting her musical heritage by chasing a more global sound
"People have a certain template they think I should follow, and it's like, you cannot tell me how to dream," she says.
"I'm able to honour my culture, but also try new things, because that's who I am."
Starr answers her critics, in a roundabout way, on her album cover - where she pairs a club-ready gold dress with a traditional gele headwrap.
"I wanted young girls in Kwara State or Erin-Ile to see this and feel represented," she told Capital Xtra, external.
"I'm not the first to do it, I won't be the last to do it - but I want people to feel confident in their culture and wear [the gele] like the crown that it is."
Not for the first time, her instincts proved right. Starr's stunning, retro-futuristic look has gone viral, inspiring dozens of copycats, and tempering at least some of the criticism of her new direction.
As she says in her new song, Amazing: "If they're gonna talk, I'll give them something to talk about".
"That's definitely my mantra," she says.
"And do you know what? I think I need to listen to myself more because I have all the answers in my music."

title: Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'Vulture King' is fighting to reverse the trend
summary: Some see them as sinister or hunt them for ritual use but these birds play a vital role in nature's cycle.
full_text:
Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'Vulture King' is fighting to reverse the trend
- Published
"People fear the environment where the shrine is. No evil will ever happen here. So, nobody fights vultures that perch here," a man they call the Vulture King tells the BBC.
Mostly associated with death and decay, perhaps it is not surprising that when vultures disappeared from the skies across many West African cities, they were not missed.
Yet across the continent, their disappearance is becoming impossible to ignore, as conservationists warn that hunting linked to traditional beliefs and spiritual practices continues to threaten several vulture species to the point of near extinction.
Without vultures, ecosystems would lose a natural defence against the spread of disease.
Thankfully in one part of south-eastern Nigeria, residents are bucking the trend.
Awka-Etiti is home to a sacred forest surrounding a shrine dedicated to a deity known as Nguma.
At first glance, the site is an unremarkable cluster of tall trees wrapped in thick greenery. But at its heart stands an ancient tree that locals say has watched over the community for hundreds of years, and remains the spiritual home of the shrine.
This is a largely Christian community but some residents continue to observe traditional practices, in which vultures play a key role.
Local resident Chukwuemeka Igwe, who has earned the nickname King of Vulture, thanks to his tireless volunteer work with Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), says "the indigenous don't hunt vultures".
Instead, locals sometimes offer fresh animal sacrifices at the shrine which attract the birds, he explains.
"And there is an adage we use here that says: 'When you put down a sacrifice and you do not see vulture[s], know that something happened in the spirit world'."
It means that vultures are a good omen when a sacrifice has been made because their presence suggests that the deity has accepted the sacrifice and heard the residents' appeal to its power.
Now in his 50s, Igwe says the birds have been a feature of daily life in this town for as long as he can remember, walking around among humans and scavenging for food.
Yet for many who venture into the wild elsewhere on the continent, vultures are not the first birds to capture their attention. Rarely do we stop to admire vultures through binoculars or photograph in awe.
In the eyes of many people, vultures are downright ugly. But scientists say they provide one of nature's most important cleaning services.
Vultures consume dead animals within hours, helping prevent carcasses from becoming breeding grounds for dangerous bacteria and diseases.
Their disappearance can have serious consequences, says NCF conservation biologist Stella Egbe: "In places where the total collapse of vultures has happened, there has been impact of rising zoonotic diseases."
Vultures' powerful stomach acids allow them to safely consume infected animals, helping stop diseases such as anthrax and rabies from spreading.
Without vultures, experts warn ecosystems lose a natural defence system.
Rapid urban growth across Africa has also played its part, transforming landscapes, and destroying many of the tall trees that the birds nest in.
Habitat loss is far from the only factor.
Poisoning is the cause of death for an estimated 60% of vultures in Africa, according to BirdLife International, external.
These issues will be high on the agenda when researchers from across the region meet in Abuja later this year to review the West African Vulture Conservation Action Plan, which was drafted in 2022.
Experts say the use of vultures and their body parts in traditional medicine and Vodun (also known as Voodoo) has emerged as one of the most significant drivers of their decline, especially in West and southern Africa.
Dead adult vultures in Nigeria used to sell for around 25,000 to 30,000 naira ($18 to $22; £13 to £16) each - but can now fetch up to 200,000 naira ($145; £107) per bird, says Egbe.
Vulture eggs and nests are increasingly targeted too, which for such a slow-breeding species is a catastrophic and "shocking" development, says Egbe.
Adult vultures usually reach sexual maturity between the ages of five and seven, and produce only one chick every year or two. Plus many young vultures do not survive their first year.
"And so you imagine what will happen if a nest is removed and eggs are removed. That means a pair of vultures will not have a next generation for that year. So in addition to hunting, you're removing their habitat, you're removing their homes," she adds.
Seven species of vultures in Africa are now classified as globally Endangered or Critically Endangered by BirdLife International, the authority for birds on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
A recent BirdLife report says African vulture populations have fallen by between 80% and 97% over a period of 50 years.
The group also says that in January 2020 more than 2,000 hooded vultures were found dead in Guinea-Bissau, many with their heads removed - a sign of belief-based practices rather than natural causes, researchers say.
As vulture populations continue to fall across the region, conservationists have been searching for communities where these birds are not hunted, feared or exploited.
They found one such example in Awka-Etiti.
Yet in recent years, Igwe says he and other residents became worried when they noticed outsiders arriving to hunt the birds and vulture numbers dwindled.
In his quest to save the birds he visits markets, buses and public spaces to spread the word: "I tell them that vulture is helpful to human life".
He says he "cannot run away" from his unusual nickname of Ezeudene, or the King of Vulture.
"I'm fighting to make nature exist the way it's supposed to be."
Working with the NCF for the past six years, Igwe has mobilised community leaders, local groups and security teams to protect the birds from outside hunters, with local bylaws now helping to formalise their protection.
Local volunteers monitoring the birds say they have now recorded more than 160 vultures, up from about 20 recorded in 2017.
We've heard shocking news that people are not just going for vultures anymore, they're going for the nests and even the eggs."
Nigeria has become a major hub for the illegal trade of vultures, conservationists say, partly because of its biodiversity and porous borders.
"We are doing everything possible to make sure that the smuggling of items, including vultures, including donkeys, and other species outside the country is suppressed to the barest minimum," insists Abdullahi Maiwada, a spokesman for the Nigerian Customs Service.
He says customs officials have carried out seizures of protected wildlife and supported prosecutions linked to illegal trafficking.
It is an example of how Nigeria is trying to live up its commitments as a member of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites) - under which endangered species are not allowed to be traded across borders.
But Maiwada admits to the BBC that enforcement alone is not enough - education will be crucial too.
"We may not be able to do it without the cooperation or understanding of members of the community," he continues. "If people understand why these species should be preserved, then our enforcement will only be complementary to those who decide to be recalcitrant."
That message has been at the heart of conservation work in Awka-Etiti and across parts of Nigeria.
Although reliable population data remains limited, conservationists say there are encouraging signs in Awka-Etiti, with local engagement helping residents become vigilant against outside hunters.
"The missing vultures are almost back. If you go to the marketplace now, you see vultures. At one time they disappeared, but now they are coming back," Igwe confirms.

title: The Papers: 'The Sun, the Moon' and 'The greatest show on Earth'
summary: The once in a generation solar eclipse across the UK and Europe dominates Thursday's front pages.
full_text: 'The Sun, the Moon' and 'The greatest show on Earth'Published2 hours agoImage caption, The once-in-a-generation solar eclipse spanning the UK and Europe dominates Thursday's front pages. The Sun splashes on a striking image of a partial eclipse leaving a crescent sliver peeking out with the playful headline: "The Sun, the Moon." And, yes, it does cheekily employ its own famous masthead as part of the very special effect.Image caption, "Once in a generation" is the i Paper's headline as it fills its front page with an image of the Moon completely obscuring the Sun, which was what was seen in parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain.Image caption, "Hello darkness my old friend" says Metro, showing the Moon slowly blotting out the Sun as seen in the skies above south London, where a 97% eclipse was witnessed.Image caption, "Move over, sunshine" says the Independent, noting that the eclipse brought a "moment of shade" to the ongoing heatwave.Image caption, The Daily Mail strikes a similar note, saying the UK "finally gets a break from the sun" during the eclipse, albeit "only for a few minutes". Alongside, the paper's top story says climate campaigners are criticising the government's environment policies for the more than 1,000 wildfires this year.Image caption, The Daily Telegraph calls the solar eclipse "the greatest show on Earth", picturing a crowd in Birmingham gazing at the phenomenon along with millions across the UK and Europe. Among its other top stories, the paper says Vladimir Putin has threatened to seize British ships in retaliation for a European crackdown on Russia's shadow fleet. A UK government spokesman says the UK Armed Forces are disrupting harmful activity of shadow fleet vessels and "operate firmly in line with international maritime law".Image caption, The Times follows with its own photo of the eclipse seen from Spain, saying it was the most significant eclipse in more than 25 years. In politics news, it reports that the PM's proposals to restrict zero hours contracts could impose costs up to £3bn a year on businesses.Image caption, "Solar eclipse thrills Europe" says the Financial Times. Elsewhere, the paper says Ukraine has halted its drone strikes on oil tankers using a critical Russian port in the Black Sea after a request from US Vice-President JD Vance.Image caption, With more on climate, the Guardian reports the PM is promising to tackle "the bigger questions" of climate adaptation, the nurses unions warning that their staff were collapsing during shifts amid conditions caused by extreme heat.Image caption, Finally, the Daily Express covers a study that shows taking the stairs instead of the lift could cut your risk of an early death by nearly a quarter. title: I've been fighting wildfires while I wait for my A-level results
summary: Grades for A-levels and a number of vocational qualifications will be published on Thursday.
full_text:
I've been fighting wildfires while I wait for my A-level results
- Published
An 18-year-old firefighter who combined his A-levels with responding to emergency calls is among thousands of students getting results on Thursday morning.
Bobi Jones from Newcastle Emlyn in Carmarthenshire said he felt "quite relaxed" about his grades after having "plenty on my plate" responding to recent wildfires.
As well as A-levels, results for AS, BTec and other vocational qualifications will also be published, with many students hoping to progress to university.
A-level grades can be shared with students from 08:00 BST but arrangements vary depending on the school or college.
Bobi is waiting for results for A-level business and sport, as well as the Welsh Baccalaureate qualification.
He said his school, Ysgol Bro Teifi, had been "very flexible", with teachers allowing him to leave class when his work alarm went off as long as he caught up with schoolwork afterwards.
"The past few months have been very busy with exams and also the fire brigade. We've been really busy with fires and wildfires," he said.
Fortunately the problem has not been as serious as in some areas, but Bobi has been regularly responding to "a few patches of grass going up on fire and just spreading very fast".
He is now planning to take on an apprenticeship with a local electrician which he will combine with on-call shifts for Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service.
Last year, the proportion of A* grades rose slightly to 10.5%, while 29.5% of results were A or A* which was lower than in 2024.
Data shows 32.8% of Welsh 18-year-olds had applied for university places by the end of June - slightly up on last year but lower than figures for other UK nations.
Rosa MacGowan, 18, from Swansea juggled studying four A-levels and the Welsh Baccalaureate alongside her part-time job in the hope of going on to be a doctor.
Having spent the summer Interrailing and spending time with friends, she is eager to find out what's next.
"My first choice is to study medicine at Glasgow uni, and my insurance is pharmacy at Newcastle," she said.
"I am really excited about either of these options, as they seem like really fun cities, and completely different to Swansea.
"I think both of these courses should have good career prospects, and lots of interesting opportunities."
Rosa said she felt "positive about the future and can't wait for the next chapter".
"I am nervous for results day, but I am aware that if it doesn't work out, there's plenty of other options, and I can always go travelling again".
William Hopkins has been studying for a BTEC in Uniformed Protective Services, alongside his A-levels and hopes to join the Army after results day.
"I've enjoyed it, but I've never been really academic and I never really enjoyed school that much," he said.
"I think I'll still get decent-ish grades but I could have probably done a bit more.
"I'm looking to go into either the Army or Royal Marines as an officer."
William wants to follow in the footsteps of family members by joining the armed forces and some of his friends signed up at 16.
"They've all gone in younger, but I wanted to have a bit more experience living I guess," he added.
"I've always enjoyed new things and testing my limits.
"Even if I don't get into the Army I know I will land on my feet somewhere else."
Aiming for a place studying criminology with psychology at the University of the West of England in Bristol, Caitlin Giffard, also from Swansea, needs three Bs.
She did well in last year's AS results so feels hopeful.
"It was a real eye-opener, really, the difference between GCSE and A-level, because I had a lot of friends who did quite well at GCSEs, but then had grades drop at A-level.
"I think it shows how big the jump was.
"I felt good about my exams though this year, so I'm hoping for good results."
Caitlin said she felt "quite positive "about the future despite the unknown of results day being "a little scary".
Results for the Advanced Skills Baccalaureate Wales will also be released on Thursday.
Many students will need confirmation of their grades to secure university offers and can usually get updated information about their places, external from 08:00 BST.
The most popular A-level subjects this year were still mathematics, biology, chemistry and psychology.
According to provisional data for summer 2026, the largest proportional decreases in entries compared to 2025 were in computer science (-14.9%), Spanish (-12.9%) and drama and theatre (-8.2%).
English language and literature entries increased by 23.3%, Welsh language was up 42.7%, while German, from a small base, increased by 59.4%.
Fewer 16-year-olds in Wales have been going on to study A-levels in recent years according to data from Medr, the body which oversees and funds post-16 education.
Provisional data for 2025/26 suggested that less than half (49%) of Year 11 students who carry on in education now progress to AS courses, the first year of A-levels, compared with 60% in 2014/15.
Figures show a growing proportion are going on to study Level 2 courses, which are equivalent to GCSE, rather than a Level 3 course.

Bethan Evans, executive director for regulation and analysis at Medr, said there had been a drop in the number of students progressing to study at A-level "particularly in the years since Covid".
Asked whether that was a concern, she said there were "more options available to our young people today than ever before".
"More and more people at the age of 16 are choosing to go to study vocational qualifications at further education colleges, for example," she said.
This year's results come after a major UK government report, external highlighted "shrinking" job and career opportunities for a "lost generation" of young people with high numbers not in education, employment and training (Neet).
Welsh government data suggests that 17% of Welsh young people aged 16 to 24 are Neet.
Evans said it was "a significant challenge for us" which had "an impact on people's life prospects".
She said Medr worked across universities, colleges and apprenticeship providers to try to address the issue.
"I think we do see that there is a risk of losing some learners fairly early on in their [education] journey, and that's part of the reason why Medr has put in place an expansion of the junior apprenticeship scheme," she added.

title: Ebola outbreak on track to be deadliest ever, WHO chief says
summary: The outbreak, declared on 15 May, has caused more than 2,000 deaths, with thousands more reported cases.
full_text:
Ebola outbreak on track to be deadliest ever, WHO chief says
- Published
The current outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo is on track to surpass the deadliest outbreak of the disease ever, the director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters that the 2026 outbreak, "at its current pace", would "eclipse" that of the 2014-2016 occurrence, which killed at least 11,000 people.
The outbreak this year, declared on 15 May, has seen at least 4,300 cases and caused more than 2,000 deaths.
The WHO said on Wednesday it hoped to reverse the spread of the disease within three months but warned that this meant bringing transmission under control - not ending the outbreak entirely.
The epidemic was only officially declared in May, but it is believed the outbreak began at least three months before then, health officials said this week.
"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, near the centre of the outbreak.
He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.
The 2026 outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which has previously caused only two known outbreaks - in 2007 and 2012.
No approved vaccine or recognised therapeutic drugs can treat this species of the virus.
Ongoing regional instability near the location of the outbreak, in the east of DR Congo, has added to challenges in controlling the spread of the disease. As a result, health workers are only reaching about 30% of cases, according to Janabi.
Ebola is a rare but deadly viral disease, with symptoms appearing within two to 21 days of infection.
Symptoms similar to the flu or malaria, including fever, headache and tiredness, can begin suddenly. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea can develop, leading to organ failure.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, has given permission for the first human trials of a vaccine for Bundibugyo to go ahead.
The jab is being created by a team from the University of Oxford based on the same technology used in the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine. Three other groups are also developing different vaccines for Bundibugyo although they have not yet entered clinical trials.
The WHO is also sponsoring a separate clinical trial in DR Congo to see whether two existing antiviral therapies can improve survival rates.

title: Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions
summary: Monica Lennon, Joe Fagan and Michael Marra are competing to fill the post vacated by Anas Sarwar.
full_text:
Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions
- Published
Scottish Labour leadership contenders have warned about the dangers of internal feuds and briefings at their first party hustings in Glasgow.
Monica Lennon, Joe Fagan and Michael Marra made their cases to succeed Anas Sarwar as they pitched to rebuild Scottish Labour after May's crushing electoral defeat.
Those attending the hour-long event were met by a handful of pro-Palestine protesters, whose shouts were heard during the first part of the event.
All three candidates promised to change, rebuild and unite the party following its worst Holyrood election defeat since devolution.
- Nominations open in Scottish Labour leadership contest 
  - Published3 August
- What does Andy Burnham mean for Scottish Labour? 
  - Published17 July
Labour came joint second in the May poll, tied with Reform on 17 seats each.
Sarwar vowed to stay on in the immediate aftermath of the result, but just two months later announced his intention to stand down as both Scottish leader and MSP to join Andy Burnham's government.
Sarwar's resignation triggered the current leadership contest. Nominations close on 17 August, with party members and affiliated supporters voting between 28 August and 17 September.
Lennon: 'Factionalism, dirty tricks and smears'
Speaking in Glasgow on Wednesday evening, Lennon warned the party in Scotland was experiencing its "worst ever crisis".
"The choice is stark," she told members.
"Either continue with the old ways that lost, or choose a leader with the vision, courage and empathy to make it electable."
The Glasgow MSP - who returned to Holyrood after taking up Sarwar's vacated list seat - said she owed it to members to ensure Scottish Labour did not "sleepwalk into electoral oblivion", urging the party to get "out of this coma".
Lennon made a plea for unity but said the party had to change, saying the "public don't believe us when we say we are Scottish Labour".
She also said she would not be "bullied" or "intimidated by those putting party control above principles" and warned against "factionalism, dirty tricks and smears".
'Negative, cowardly briefings' - Marra
Marra also warned against "negative cowardly briefings", saying those who believed they could win votes were "dangerously deluded".
He said Scottish Labour had "refused to see" the election defeat coming and had failed to stop successive election losses, despite what he described as a "feckless, incompetent and corrupt SNP".
The North East MSP told the crowd that the party's problems were "much deeper than structures", adding that the party "must change our culture".
He said the next leader needed to "renew" the party and "rediscover its moral purpose".
In his closing remarks, Marra said the leadership contest was about choosing the candidate best able to "bring the party together" and "galvanise that movement".
He warned: "If we don't change, we'll be here again in five years. And how's that going to feel?"
Fagan - 'learn to win again'
Fagan said Scottish Labour had to "change more than the faces at the top".
The South Scotland MSP said the party had to be bold and get "squarely on the side of the working people of this country".
"I am standing to unite our party, to back our movement, to seize this moment and rebuild Scottish Labour as a party for working people of Scotland," he said.
Fagan said Scottish Labour needed to rediscover its "courage, boldness and imagination".
"Let Scottish Labour decay, and when Labour decays, Scotland decays," he said.
He called "caution and division" the party's "deadly enemies", saying "boldness, courage and unity are our only path".
He also said Labour needed to "learn to win again", arguing that it succeeded when it was "rooted in communities and serious about people's lives".
The new leader is due to be announced on 19 September.

title: How to get the most out of university clearing on results day
summary: From listing potential outcomes to picking up the phone, these are some top tips for getting through clearing.
full_text:
How to get the most out of university clearing on results day
- Published
Have you changed your mind about the university course you want to start after getting your results?
Maybe you did not apply to university originally but now want to go, or you might not end up getting the grades you need to make it into your firm choice.
If that is you, the clearing process will have you covered.
While students in Scotland received their results last week, young people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will find out how they did in their exams on Thursday 13 August.
Here is everything you need to know about clearing.
What is clearing?
Clearing is how universities and colleges fill any places that they still have on their courses and how students can change their course or place of study.
This year, clearing runs from 2 July to 19 October.
Prospective students can use clearing if:
- You are applying after 30 June
- You did not receive any offers (or none you wanted to accept)
- You did not meet the conditions on your offers
- You have declined your firm place using the "decline my place" button in your application
- You are not already holding any offer from a university or college, and the course still has places
- You want to go to your insurance choice instead of your firm. You will have to check in clearing whether your insurance choice will accept you
- You have done better than expected and want to go to a different university
What can students do to prepare for clearing?
Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing.
She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes.
For example, depending on available places:
- If I get AAA, then I could do physics at Sussex
- BBC could be physics at Aberystwyth
- CCD could be physics at Nottingham Trent
If you are doing BTecs, T-levels or other qualifications, you can work out how many Ucas points your results are worth using the calculator tool on their website, external.
The Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here, external. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.
For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher.
She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.
She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.
Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people.
At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades".
On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history.
"The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says.
"That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.
For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day.
That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade.
"You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says.
"Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."
Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact.
"Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says.
"With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."
How does it work and what do you need to do on results day?
For those awaiting results, Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your grades.
But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website.
"I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."
Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand.
On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it.
"It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford.
"All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."
Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available.
"Work up a priority list," he says.
"For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."
Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person.
She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities.
"I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says.
"You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."
Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.
How long do you have to decide on an offer?
Bradford says many students "can't afford" to spend days ruminating on their offer as popular courses do get filled quickly, but it is important to not agree to one straight away.
"Spend a small amount of time thinking, what do I really want from my experience? Don't panic buy and accept the first offer that comes along."
Wade says students need to ask their preferred university how much time they have to accept the offer on results day as every university is different.
"The more super-selective the university, the less time they will have," she says.
"Generally, I would always say sleep on it. Most universities will give students some time, but ask that question on the phone."
Clarification 12 August: This article was amended to include further details about the process for Scottish students which were omitted from the previous version.

title: Zimbabwe’s land reform enters a new chapter
summary: A new land policy is reopening disputes over farms seized during Zimbabwe’s land reform after 2000.
full_text:
Zimbabwe’s land reform enters a new chapter
A new land policy is reopening disputes over farms seized during Zimbabwe’s land reform after 2000.
Harare, Zimbabwe – More than two decades after Zimbabwe seized thousands of mainly white-owned commercial farms, some of those properties are set to change hands again.
But President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s government insisted the move is not a reversal of the land redistribution programme that reshaped Zimbabwe’s countryside after 2000.
Instead, officials said they are resolving three separate categories of land claims involving foreign investors, Black Zimbabwean owners and white farmers who remained on acquired land.
Sixty-seven farms protected by bilateral investment promotion and protection agreements (BIPPAs) are being returned to investors from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Another 840 farms that officials said were included in the acquisition process in error during land reform are to be restored to their Black Zimbabwean owners.
And 409 white farmers who have remained on farms alongside land reform beneficiaries will be allowed to buy the farms or portions they occupy through a set-off mechanism linked to compensation for eligible improvements.
“The BIPPA process is about resolving outstanding legal obligations relating to investments protected under bilateral agreements. It should not be mistaken for a return to the pre-land reform era,” Agriculture Minister Anxious Masuka told Parliament.
The distinction matters because land remains one of Zimbabwe’s most politically charged issues, closely tied to the colonial era and the liberation struggle.
A colonial legacy
At independence in 1980, white commercial farmers controlled a disproportionate share of Zimbabwe’s most productive farmland, reflecting colonial policies that restricted Black Zimbabweans’ access to prime agricultural land.
Under the Lancaster House settlement, redistribution initially operated largely on a “willing buyer, willing seller” basis with Britain helping finance parts of the early programme.
But redistribution was slower than many Black Zimbabweans expected.
In February 2000, voters rejected a government-backed constitutional referendum that would have expanded the state’s powers to acquire land. Soon afterwards, war veterans and supporters of the ZANU-PF party, which has governed Zimbabwe since independence, began occupying white-owned farms.
The government formalised the occupations through the Fast-Track Land Reform Programme (FTLRP).
Supporters saw the seizures as the unfinished business of independence. Human Rights Watch documented violence, intimidation and political discrimination during the process while disputes over ownership and allocation continued for years.
The upheaval severely disrupted commercial agriculture and contributed to Zimbabwe’s wider economic crisis, which had multiple causes, including monetary and fiscal problems, drought and other policy failures.
More than two decades later, Zimbabwe is still grappling with the competing claims that upheaval created.
Three categories
The policy distinguishes between three categories of claimants, each with a different legal and political basis.
The 67 BIPPA-protected farms involve foreign investors whose investments were covered by bilateral agreements. Officials said the properties were designated for compulsory acquisition during land reform but remained unoccupied and are being returned to investors as Zimbabwe addresses its obligations under those agreements.
The second group is 840 farms that officials said were included in the acquisition process in error during land reform. They are to be restored to their Black Zimbabwean owners.
The third comprises 409 white farmers who have remained on farms alongside land reform beneficiaries. They will be allowed to buy the farms or portions they currently occupy rather than simply receiving them back.
Taken together, the three categories illustrate how Zimbabwe’s land question has become increasingly complex with competing claims rooted in different legal, political and historical foundations.
‘We could have done it better’
Milton Gurajena, a war veteran who participated in the farm occupations, remembered them as a national mobilisation.
“We just went into the farms, guided by the national fever. It was just arriving at the farm and giving the owner little notice. Our aim was to take our land back. Oftentimes, the big guys would take it from us and advise us to find another farm,” he said.
But he acknowledged that many participants did not understand the legal consequences.
“We did not have much knowledge except party directives and the common line that ‘we are taking our land back.’ Of course, we had some grievances, but when I look back, we could have done it better and more orderly without turning the process into a war,” he said.
His account reflects the central tension of the land reform: A programme intended to correct a historical injustice was itself marked by violence, political pressure and legal uncertainty.
Investment pressure
For Mnangagwa’s government, the land decisions are not only about resolving historical disputes; they are also part of a broader effort to rebuild relations with Western governments and international lenders.
Zimbabwe is seeking debt relief, renewed access to international financing and improved investor confidence. Analysts have linked the return of the BIPPA-protected farms to those broader efforts to improve the country’s investment climate and relations with international creditors.
The BIPPA process is separate from Zimbabwe’s $3.5bn compensation framework for eligible former commercial farmers, agreed in 2020. That programme covers improvements made to farms acquired by the state while ownership of the land remains with the state.
Zimbabwe began making payments under that framework in 2025, but the government has faced financial constraints in meeting the wider commitment.
At the same time, the government said it is issuing title deeds to farmers who benefitted from land reform, seeking to give them greater security of tenure and encourage investment. Officials insisted that land reform itself remains irreversible.
A return to the farm
For some former owners, the latest moves have revived hopes of regaining access to properties they lost more than two decades ago.
Michael Kwaramba, a second-generation heir to his family’s estate, said his father suffered after the farm was mistakenly designated for compulsory acquisition by the state during land reform.
“He went through a lot when our farm was wrongly gazetted, which I think contributed to his untimely death. We have been waiting for years, and the announcement is encouraging,” he said.
Willem Jansen, a Dutch-born Zimbabwean farmer now based in South Africa, also hopes to regain his family’s farm.
“Hopefully, I will get my land back. It was our family land, and we had created an ecosystem that even after our forced removal, farm workers and nearby villages were affected, lost jobs and opportunities we were creating together,” he said.
But for those who fought for land reform, the prospect of former owners regaining a foothold on the land remains difficult.
Marko Dzingirai, a war veteran, said he was unsure what the changes would mean for farmers who settled on land after the reform.
“Just like in the beginning when we invaded the farms, we did not know about the existence of all these treaties and agreements on the farms. So now, I don’t know if the farm here is part of the BIPPA or not,” he said.
“We supported the party because of moves like these. Hopefully, they are not betraying our sacrifices,” he said.

title: Nearly 200-country study shows China’s Belt and Road Initiative cuts debt and corruption
summary:
A study analysing data from hundreds of countries and regions suggests China’s Belt and Road Initiative is linked to better governance and economic development, according to researchers from Nanjing University.
They found the trade and investment scheme – which spans Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond – was also associated with improved corruption control and that it reduced debt risks.
The team – from the university’s Centre for Asia-Pacific Development Studies and led by Mao Weizhun – said their...
full_text:
Nearly 200-country study shows China’s Belt and Road Initiative cuts debt and corruption
Data analysis spanning more than 20 years across 197 countries and regions challenges ‘debt trap diplomacy’ narrative
They found the trade and investment scheme – which spans Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond – was also associated with improved corruption control and that it reduced debt risks.
The team – from the university’s Centre for Asia-Pacific Development Studies and led by Mao Weizhun – said their findings challenged characterisations of the trade and infrastructure initiative as a “failure”, “vulnerability trap”, “road of corruption” or a “debt trap”.
They published their research in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Quarterly Journal of International Politics in late July.
The study involved analysis of data from 197 countries and regions between 2000 and 2023. That included 146 countries that signed belt and road cooperation agreements with China and 135 countries where belt and road infrastructure projects had been launched or completed.
Critics have said the initiative – launched in 2013 – lacks transparency, that the projects fuel unsustainable debt, exploit workers, cause environmental damage and are used by Beijing to wield influence.

title: Reformers were ‘spectacularly unsuccessful’ in taking over NSW Liberals, Catholic schools boss says
summary:
Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney tells Icac corruption inquiry that Christain factional group driven by ‘a calling … a duty’

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A factional ally of the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has told a corruption inquiry a group of Christian Liberal power brokers who allegedly solicited illegal political donations were “spectacularly unsuccessful in their ambitions”.

The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, told the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption on Thursday that the Reformers’ model was never correct.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A factional ally of the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has told a corruption inquiry a group of Christian Liberal power brokers who allegedly solicited illegal political donations were “spectacularly unsuccessful in their ambitions”.
The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, told the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption on Thursday that the Reformers’ model was never correct.
Icac is investigating whether McInerney arranged and approved donations from the governing body for 600 Catholic schools to support alleged branch stacking efforts of the conservative Christian group.
The Reformers wanted more conservative policies on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia. A document drafted around the group’s inception proposed to recruit 5,000 Christian conservatives to join NSW Liberal party branches “and thereby take control of the NSW division of the Liberal party”.
McInerney on Thursday admitted he first became aware of Reformers’ recruitment events in late 2018 and 2019. He said he was “mostly” supportive of their goals.
Counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, asked: “What’s the qualification here, Mr McInerney?”
“They were spectacularly unsuccessful in their ambitions,” he replied. “I never thought the model was right.”
McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he previously said in a statement.
McInerney on Thursday accepted he had begun to speak frequently to Reformers Christian Ellis, Robert Assaf and Jean-Claude Perrottet by 2020. Asked if he knew that the men were “fervent” in the pursuit of the Reformers’ goals, McInerney said the word was “very subjective”.
Asked if “passionate” was a better word, he said: “I actually don’t think there was a passion there. I think it was a calling for them, a duty.”
Nearly 80% of funding managed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from federal and state funding, or about $3.8bn in 2024.
Icac has previously heard that Catholic Schools NSW paid monthly retainers to two lobbying firms controlled by members of the Reformers for consulting services.
It paid Beckington, run by Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, $130,900 between August 2019 and August 2021, and JPG Advisory, run by Greenwood, $135,000 between December 2021 and December 2023.
During evidence on Wednesday, Greenwood, who has disputed whether he was a member of the Reformers, was read messages between himself and McInerney in October 2022 in which the latter asked about missing invoices. Greenwood responded: “I stopped sending them in the end haha.”
The counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked why he had signed off the message in that way: “Is the joke on parents paying funds to Catholic Schools NSW, or the government assisting with that funding, that this money is not for any genuine consultancy, but was in fact intended in part to fund Jean-Claude Perrottet?”
“Absolutely not,” Greenwood replied.
On Thursday, the inquiry heard that McInerney, the only CEO of Catholic Schools NSW since its founding in 2017, joined the Liberal party while at school in the late 1980s or early 1990s. He remained a member until June this year, when he also ceased being the president of the Mittagong branch.
McInerney, a member of the Liberals right faction, came to know senior conservative state and federal parliamentarians including Tony Abbott, Angus Taylor, Matt Canavan, Dominic Perrottet and Damien Tudehope. McInerney and right faction members later spoke at Reformers events.
He said the right faction members had “uniform awareness and knowledge” about the Reformers’ work, but were “not uniformly supportive in acceptance”.
In its first week, the inquiry heard a message sent by McInerney, who is a factional ally of Taylor, to Assaf in March 2021, advising of a plan to “shake down Angus for 10K”.
Taylor has not been named in Icac’s allegations and has repeatedly denied he ever made payments to the Reformers.
McInerney admitted to having his own political ambitions “off and on for several” years, but said he was “at peace” with not taking over the late federal Liberal senator Jim Molan’s seat. Molan died in January 2023 but McInerney missed out on the Senate spot.
He was read messages exchanged between him and Greenwood in which he wrote: “I know I’ve been fucked.”
“Yeah it’s fucked, it’s fucked, it’s fucked,” McInerney wrote in March 2023.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

title: Telstra CEO gets $700,000 pay rise to $6.8m despite Australia-wide outage
summary:
Telco board cuts senior executive bonuses by total $1.3m after tech fail that affected millions

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Telstra has paid its chief executive, Vicki Brady, $6.8m for the year ending in June, after docking 20% of her bonus in response to the network’s nationwide outage in July.

The company reported financial results on Thursday. Its board met on Monday and decided to cut Brady’s bonus by $607,000 – but she still took home a $700,000 pay rise as she was awarded a total of $6.1m the year before.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Telstra has paid its chief executive, Vicki Brady, $6.8m for the year ending in June, after docking 20% of her bonus in response to the network’s nationwide outage in July.
The company reported financial results on Thursday. Its board met on Monday and decided to cut Brady’s bonus by $607,000 – but she still took home a $700,000 pay rise as she was awarded a total of $6.1m the year before.
Telstra has faced heavy political criticism for its handling of the outage, which it has blamed on the lack of a software update on a key time-keeping system. The incident was estimated to have affected almost half of all calls and data sessions on its network before it was traced and repaired.
Brady told investors on Thursday more than 30,000 customers had asked for compensation and nearly $1m had been paid out. The company reported it was still assessing customer claims, and was paying compensation to those who were eligible.
“At this stage regulatory outcomes and any financial implications from this outage are uncertain and cannot be reliably estimated,” the financial report read.
Brady acknowledged the outage in comments to investors on Thursday, saying that Telstra had “let our customers down in July” and had taken full accountability.
“We have an initial understanding of the root cause of the outage and have taken steps to address that,” she said. “We are completing our investigation with an external expert, and we will be transparent about those findings and the actions we take as a result.”
Brady said the company was taking the disruption “extremely seriously” and was committed to giving people clear information and fixing issues as quickly as possible.
Telstra also docked 20% of the bonus for its former global networks group executive, and 10% of all other senior executives, cutting their combined pay by the equivalent of $1.3m. The company’s results show senior executives were paid a combined $20.7m for the year.
Brady told reporters there was a “small impact” in customers leaving the telco following July’s outage, but ultimately “no material impact” on customers leaving or new customers signing up.
“I don’t take that for granted, nor do any of the team at Telstra.”
Wednesday’s earnings results showed profits rose to $2.4bn, from $2.3bn the prior year. It paid shareholders a dividend of 21 cents per share.
Telstra has cut costs by cutting jobs: employee numbers fell by 1,219 over the year to a total 29,334 by June.
Income from mobile phones rose $300m to $11.3bn, with customers paying an extra 7.2% on prepaid handheld plans and an extra 3.4% on postpaid handheld plans. The company increased most of its postpaid plans by $4 a month and prepaid by $5 a month in May.
Telstra sold 1m more mobile plans despite rising prices and now has 26m services in operation.
However, following multiple price increases, much of the company’s growth in subscribers is being driven through prepaid and its wholesale business, which sells Telstra’s mobile network under brands including Woolworths and Aldi. Brady called this the “value-conscious end of the market”.
Telstra reported a drop in postpaid subscriptions directly with Telstra of 7,000 in the financial year, compared to 46,000 additions in pre-paid, and 235,000 in wholesale.
Brady said the wholesale offers give customers “a lot of choice… because we fully appreciate and understand that cost of living is a big pressure on a lot of people in the country.”
The company’s share price slipped from $5 to $4.875 in early trading, dragging its market value down by $1.4bn to hit $54.3bn.

full_text:
David McBride, the former army lawyer jailed for his role in stealing secret defence documents about the Afghanistan war and leaking them to the media, has been released from prison in Canberra on Thursday.
McBride was sentenced to a maximum five years and eight months in jail in May 2024, but is being released on parole after serving his full non-parole period of 27 months.
McBride pleaded guilty to three charges in November after the ACT supreme court upheld a commonwealth intervention to withhold key evidence the government argued had the potential to jeopardise “the security and defence of Australia”. The charges included stealing commonwealth information and passing that on to journalists at the ABC.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, approved McBride’s release on Thursday.
A spokesperson for Rowland confirmed his release to Guardian Australia.
“Mr McBride’s parole was considered and granted,” the spokesperson said.
“The government does not provide specific commentary or details about individual parole matters.”
McBride released a statement after the decision, thanking Rowland “for sparing us another long fight over the question of parole.”
“After all we both want the same thing, a better Australia for our children, so it seems a waste to be fighting each other, rather than working together,” he said.
He said he would make a more comprehensive statement at a later date and acknowledged his family, prison officers and his fellow inmates.
McBride also revealed he was diagnosed with treatable lung cancer, currently in its early stages. He is expected to undergo surgery imminently.
“Many thanked me for allowing them to believe in this country again, in turn, I thank them for showing me there are so many good people in the world worth fighting for,” he said.
McBride collected mostly secret military information over an 18-month period in 2014 and 2015 and handed it to journalists at the public broadcaster. The material was used as the basis for an investigative series exposing war crimes committed by Australian defence personnel in Afghanistan titled The Afghan Files.
The court heard a total of 235 documents were taken by McBride from defence offices – mostly in the ACT – between May 2014 and December 2015 with 207 of them classified as secret and some marked as cabinet documents.
Former independent senator and transparency campaigner Rex Patrick said McBride would walk away from prison with his head held high.
“David served Australians, both in the Army and in his brave act of blowing the whistle on war crimes that took place in Afghanistan. It’s so good to see the end of an awful saga that should never have happened.”
The Information Rights Project founder, Gabriel Shipton, praised the government for the decision, as well as for assistance provided to his brother, Julian Assange.
“David shouldn’t have gone to prison in the first place, but freeing a whistleblower will not go un-noticed,” Shipton said.
“It’s real-world outcomes like these that make a difference to the lives of courageous individuals who blow the whistle. A massive shout-out to all those who supported David through his epic battle for justice.”
